items.title: Ordinal Bounty #0: 100,000 sats for a single sat whose ordinal ends with a 0
items.text:
Ordinal numbers are serial numbers for satoshis. In an effort get people interested, I've been offering bounties on specific ordinals, or ordinals with specific qualities. I had a huge grab bag of bounties, but I decided to change it up and focus on one bounty at a time.

The current bounty is [here](https://ordinals.com/bounties)!

To claim the bounty, send a single sat* to the address on the bounty page. The catch: The sat must be the first sat in the output you send. This is stipulated because otherwise, sending at least 10 contiguous sats would be sufficient to claim the bounty, and that would be too easy.

To claim the bounty, you'll have to understand [how ordinals work](https://github.com/casey/ord/blob/master/bip.mediawiki), look up some ordinals you own on the [ordinals.com block explorer](ordinals.com) and write some pretty simple code to construct a transaction with input sand outputs in the right order.

NB Whenever you look up a utxo you own on a block explorer, it's a privacy leak! You can run your own copy of the block explorer, get the code [on github](https://github.com/casey/ord).

The reward is 100,000 sats**.

The bounty can only be claimed once, and is definitely unclaimed as long as no transactions have been sent to the bounty address.

The bounty page contains instructions on how to claim the bounty.

If anyone claims this bounty, I'll come up with another, harder one. Maybe one day the bounty will be to find one of the [three](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′336″0‴) [epic](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′672″0‴) [ordinals](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′1008″0‴) mined so far.

\* In practice you'll have to send more, so your transaction doesn't have dust outputs, and thus be non-standard and not relayed.

items.title: Resolvr: a Bounty Marketplace that takes the Agent out of Escrow
items.text:
Recently, a popular bounty marketplace, BountySource, [stopped paying out bounties](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1586) to developers. Many users reported outstanding or significantly delayed payouts.  [[1](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1539)] [[2](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900)]. The entities or persons running BountySource likely misused the escrowed funds being held for bounties.  Bounty posters and developers have been searching for an alternative. 

But the risk of exit scams or insolvency are inherent to all centralzied escrow agent.  That's why most jurisdictions place onerous fiduciary duties on escrow agents to faithfully hold funds for safekeeping and deliver them according to the terms of the deal.   But it can take time and money to get compensation through the courts and usually recovery is for pennies on the dollar. The costs of legal action outweighs any bounty amounts lost through embezzlement.   

So some existing platforms, like Algora, don't bother with escrow.  But, as one former BountySource user [pointed out](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900#issuecomment-1771603383), that just shifts the trust to the bounty grantor.

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/65395e3087238f2bcef5379f/9d1297aa-6072-41b9-bea3-a57814b2dee1/more+trust+in+donor.png?content-type=image%2Fpng)

Replit provides a bounty marketplace that does escrow bounty funds, but payouts are not instant or free.  Users are awarded Replit's token (cycles) for solving bounties, and must request payout in USD by email.  Users are charged a 25% withdrawal fee for any bounty funds earned, and there is a minimum withdrawal amount of $350. So, not only are you trusting that Replit won't go bankrupt, you are paying through the nose for that risk. 

[Resolvr](https://www.resolvr.io) takes the centralized agent out of escrow.  It doesn't control or possesses the bounty funds.  Instead, Resolvr leverages bitcoin's native programmability to attest to whether the bounty has been solved, triggering payout automatically.  This removes the need to trust the platform or grantor.

And Resolvr doesn't decide whether the bounty has been solved;  a panel of crowdsourced developers performs the review.   

Resolvr is the first bounty marketplace to offer dependable escrow and payouts, as well as transparent dispute resolution.  Oh, and it's cheaper than the existing alternatives.

You can [sign up](https://www.resolvr.io/) to be an alpha tester today! And check out the [GitHub](https://github.com/Resolvr-io) and join the conversation on [discord](https://discord.gg/DsqRw8My4m).

Get your bounties ready!

items.title: Intel Ends Its $100,000 Bug Bounty Program
items.text: Intel has officially suspended its Bug Bounty Program, which offered security researchers compensation for finding and reporting security vulnerabilities. The program is now marked as suspended on the Intigriti platform, but Intel has not provided a detailed explanation for this decision. Previously, Intel organized a series of bounties for those discovering bugs and vulnerabilities, divided into four tiers. In tier one, the highest payout was $5,000; tier two offered $10,000; tier three provided $30,000; and the most severe bugs in tier four could be compensated with $100,000. Tier four was intended for major vulnerability disclosures, like Spectre or Meltdown, which were significant security issues a few years ago.

items.title: The September 19 Attack — facts, full story, and a bounty (up to 3.3BTC)
items.text:
Blink was attacked on September 19 and briefly paused services https://stacker.news/items/1576826/r/Scoresby, https://stacker.news/items/1577330/r/Scoresby.

> An attacker opened an ordinary free Blink account on 17 September. Two days later they used a flaw in how our administrative tools checked permissions to give that account admin powers. With those powers they changed the email address or phone number on 35 accounts, logged in to them as if they were the owner, raised withdrawal limits on 14 of them, and withdrew bitcoin from 24 of them between 09:51 and 11:54 UTC, partly on-chain and partly over Lightning through the flow we built to help customers move to self-custody. The attacker got about 6.61 BTC.

Two-factor saved the people who had it enabled. Blink has covered the loss for all customers affected.

> Nine had two-factor authentication and lost nothing (see below), and the attacker took over the last two accounts only minutes before we shut the service down, so nothing moved from them. 22 of the 24 drained accounts belonged to customers; two belonged to Blink group companies. Every one was restored to its exact pre-incident balance on 24 September, with the withdrawal fees refunded, and the locked accounts were reopened from that day. Blink bears the loss.

The attackers also got some customer data:

>During the attack, they also read details of 3,817 other accounts. For some, these included a phone number or an email address. They did not see names, identity documents, addresses, passwords or seed phrases. We have written to every account holder we could reach, saying what was seen.

And now Blink is offering a bounty for information leading to the recovery of the stolen BTC:

> We will pay 25% of the value of any part of the 6.61 BTC stolen on 19 September that is recovered as a direct result of information you provide — up to about 1.65 BTC if all of it were. Another 25% of anything recovered goes to [Bitcoin Beach](https://www.bitcoinbeach.com/), [Bitcoin Ekasi](https://bitcoinekasi.com/), [Afribit Kibera](https://www.afribit.africa/) and their joint selection of Bitcoin circular economies in the Global South. If information leads to funds being frozen, the bounty is paid once those funds are returned to a wallet we control. The offer has no end date. Write to bounty@blinkbtc.com. The full terms, which govern, are at [blink.sv/bounty-terms](https://www.blink.sv/en/bounty-terms).

All in all, I think they are doing a pretty good job handling this.

items.title: Sword < Pen < Home Mining < High Hashrate Home Mining
items.text:
# I really hope they don't have CCTV at Microcenter.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161783)

> Clerk: Did you find everything you were looking for.
> Me: Big time! This should complete a project I've been working on forever and am really excited about.
> Clerk: How exciting! What's that?
> Me: It's a tabletop bitcoin miner with the iconic, "This machine kills fascists," plaque from Woody Guthrie's guitars on it.
> Clerk: OK sir, please don't kill people. Have a nice day.

Of course I'm sure they do have lots of CCTV at Micro Center, and of course I hope the kid working the register knew that Woody's statement on his guitar is just a variant of the, "The pen is mightier than the sword," maxim. I figured it'd be nice to step things up a notch and actually put it on a machine that literally makes it hard to control people.

# My Bitaxe

A few months back, someone in the Heatpunks forum was generously giving away a faulty bitaxe. I jumped on the opportunity since this whole bitcoin thing has led to an obsession with tinkering. Most of my tinkering has been with industrial mining machines because I think if enough home miners start harvesting this trash, we'll end of with more decentralized network security. The bitaxes are great for learning, but i already had a few industrial machines and had learned a lot from them.

My tinkering table:
![](https://m.stacker.news/161796)
My free bitaxe:
![](https://m.stacker.news/161787)

It didn't have a barrel jack, so I ordered one online since it had become immediately apparent that the usb power couldn't hold the amount of amperage the unit needed. However, the manufacturer of this particular Bitaxe Ultra had used their own PCB and the barrel jack I ordered didn't fit. So I ran the spade connectors to a barrel-to-screw terminal.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161788)

Even with the barrel jack, I had to try three separate power supplies (the first died immediately and the second couldn't hold five amps like it said it could) before I was able to get the thing running.

# My Guitaxe

So I figured, that this is *actually* stopping fascists from doing fascist things. Let's label it properly.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161793)

I just threw some jumper wires between the machines and it's screen and was able to make this nice little facade for it.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161791)

# I'm not actually a Woody Guthrie Fan

<sup>TLDR: I don't personally agree with Woody's ideology and don't dig his music. Feel free to skip ahead.</sup>

While I agree with his sentiment about fascists, Woody actually endorsed other types of authoritarianism, so I had to add a little to the statement so as to be perfectly clear. I figure, if you're going to alienate people, might as well make sure they're offended by what you *actually* are saying.

On top of that, I really don't like his music, except This Land Is Your Land, but that's mostly because of nostalgia. Nevertheless, I recognize the guy played a big role in shaping the American folk tradition, so this is a bit of an homage and critique/clarification at the same time.

# But does it scale?

So here is the state of my furnace at the end of last winter:

![](https://m.stacker.news/161794)

The primary issue was noise. So this year, I started off by seeing if cheap quiet fans could cut the muster.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161802)

The above photos are P19 Pros. I got them in bulk for $3.50 a piece. They are slightly quieter, but definitely don't do any favors to the machine efficiency.

# To Infinity and Beyond

So I finally bit the bullet and got a Njord board. Shout out to [IxTech](https://ixtech.xyz/)! I had been avoiding this route because, while not all that expensive if it worked, I wasn't confident I could pull if off. In that case, it was more expensive than I was willing to suffer through.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161800)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161801)

But I didn't take into account that the shroud I previously used to go into the furnace plenum was the **exact** size as the AC Infinity exhaust.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161803)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161804)

So, I figured since I had to make another shroud anyway, it was time to get Woody involved again.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161805)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161807)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161808)

Now, I'm rocking with AC Infinity efficiency, the kids can play in literally the room next door without complaining about the noise, I'm figuratively "killing fascists and other tyrants", doing it in a way that becomes significant if it catches on with other folks, and writing run on sentences all day long.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161809)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161810)

If you made it this far, thanks for following along! Let me know if you want me to make some provocative 3d print for your home mining rig.

items.title: My first Taproot Asset payment over the Lightning Network
items.text:
I made my first stablecoin payment on Lightning! I paid 2.14 USDTL for a glass bottle of Coca Cola at DCTRL, a hackspace in Vancouver, BC.

![Video of OP paying to a Lightning Address from their Taproot Asset channel](https://v.nostr.build/nPrMgh7eSyY4kCrFJAvvJu.mov)

**My setup:** I'm running `litd` in integrated mode, meaning LND, Taproot Assets and everything else runs as one binary, with a pruned Bitcoin Core backend.

**The asset channel:** The asset is USDTL, a bridged stablecoin issued by Speed Wallet. I asked Jesse of Amboss to open a channel to me from their node, but I expect to be able to do that soon through their Web UI. He opened a $3000 channel. By default my node will accept any Taproot Asset channel, but to be able to receive and send payments I have to configure an "oracle" that feeds my node price information about the channel. I'm using [Tassandra](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassandra) for this purpose, which I vibe coded half a year ago when testing edge node functionality. I expect that requirement to eventually be dropped, streamlining the process of receiving and sending.

**The edge node:** Amboss, my channel peer, by definition also acts as the edge node for my payments. That means that for every invoice I create or pay, Amboss is taking "the other side" of the trade. When I generate a Lightning invoice locally, that invoice can be paid by any Lightning wallet out there. The sender constructs a route to my node and sends satoshi, which get "swapped" by Amboss to USDTL at the last hop. Conversely, I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL from my node. I construct a route that sends USDTL to Amboss, which get forwarded as satoshi to the final destination. As this uses ordinary onion routing, Amboss can not see the origin of payments I receive, or the the destination of payments I make.

**The recipient:** The vending machine is quite simple. All items in it cost the same (CA$3), each payment unlocks exactly one bottle of any one kind. The payment is made to an LNURL printed on the front of the machine and is also reachable through the Lightning Address `coke@bitdevs.ca`. When an incoming payment is detected, the LNbits backend sends a signal to the Pi inside of the machine to unlock the bottle.

**The payment:** I am using [Tassilo](https://github.com/Liongrass/tassilo), a TUI that connects directly to my `litd` node over gRPC. I can see my channel, my inbound and outbound capacity for both the channel and the BTC. I can pay any Lightning invoice or LNURL, so I enter the address of the vending machine and hit send. The first thing I see is the details for the Lightning Address. These are in satoshi, but once I create an invoice and choose to pay with USDTL, I get an estimate for how much this will cost me, in dollars, excluding routing fees. I can now pay the invoice, and after a few seconds I receive the preimage, and the vending machine releases the drink. A coke costs CA$3 at the machine, which at the time of payment was 2,526 satoshi. But the amount I ended up paying was 2.144058 USDTL. To calculate the spread I make an invoice over 2.14 USDTL and pay it from another wallet later, which turns out to be 2528 satoshi. That's pretty much a 0% spread, generous of Amboss, and I'm very curious what this will cost me when these kinds of services roll out more broadly.

**More payments:** I also topped up my Mullvad account (4.5 EUR, \~5.07 USD) for 5.05 USDTL, added 5 USD to my Dracotel eSIM (5.05 USDTL), and bought a 20 CAD (\~14.03 USD) Safeway gift card from Bitrefill for 14.10 USDTL. The constant currency conversions are definitely not great, but mainly it makes you realize how wonky USD to satoshi exchange rates can already be, and some providers mark up their exchange rate to skim some extra bips from the consumer, or in expectation to be compensated for the costly liquidity management of their nodes.

**Conclusion:** Setting up Taproot Assets for yourself isn't very easy yet. But it's certainly not out of reach. You need your own Bitcoin and Lightning node and a specialized channel, and you can only interact with the node through the command line or a TUI so far. But once you have set it up, making and receiving payments is very smooth. I believe this stack will play an important role in spreading Lightning adoption around the world.

items.title: Invalid Bitcoin blocks: full PoW, consensus invalid
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/158419)

I’ve put together a [catalogue](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/invalid-blocks) and a corresponding [post](https://deadmanoz.xyz/posts/2026/invalid-blocks) detailing 143 Bitcoin blocks that met the required proof-of-work target but failed a consensus rule, from the 2010 overflow to two previously unreported F2Pool timestamp failures from 2026!!

The catalogue brings together the surviving evidence for each case, so anyone can independently verify which consensus rule the block broke.

A few findings:

* **The two F2Pool headers from April and July this year have timestamps roughly 7 and 14 days below their parents’ median time past.** Both were found in merge-mined auxiliary chains; neither has a known Bitcoin-side capture.
* **Auxiliary chains preserve 49 of the 143 headers**, and provide the catalogue’s only recorded observation for 35. They check their own rules, so they can preserve evidence of candidates that Bitcoin peers reject.
* **89 blocks contain the same P2SH-invalid transaction**, mined between April and July 2012. Archived transaction lists and preserved headers establish its inclusion in each.
* **127 of the 143 have no complete body.** The surviving headers, coinbases or transaction inclusion proofs, together with chain context, still establish the failures.
* Another 10 reported cases remain separate because the evidence is insufficient.

The same merge mining research also recovered roughly 1,400 stale headers new to the [stale-blocks collection](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/stale-blocks). Merge mining has proved to be a productive side channel for both stales and invalids, and monitoring those chains is essential to a holistic Bitcoin monitoring effort.

In my [merge mining monitor](https://mmm.deadmanoz.xyz/) tool you can step through all invalid-blocks discovered in the merge-mined record (note that invalid blocks are currently called error blocks, this was the language I originally used):

![](https://m.stacker.news/158420)

If you have old node files, pool logs or other records that could fill a gap, contributions and corrections are very welcome.

[https://github.com/bitcoin-data/invalid-blocks](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/invalid-blocks)

The first set of results were finished in around December 2025, and since then I've been trying to get it accepted at conferences and journals.  Unfortunately, the track record was not great.  A Bitcoin research conference did not take it (no reason given), the *Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization* did not take it (too niche), and *Electronics Commerce Research and Applications* did not take it (I don't write like an IS scholar).

But, I'm pleased to say that finally we are having some success. The paper was just accepted to the *Workshop on Information Systems and Economics*, which will be held in Lisbon, Portugal this December.  This is one of the main conferences for economists studying information systems, and the [program](https://wiseconf2026.github.io/) looks super interesting.  I think this is the right group of people to try and get this work in front of, and I'm looking forward to the feedback I get -- as well as the exposure Stacker News may receive from other researchers.

If you're interested, you can read a working draft of the paper [here](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6556022)

items.title: Distributed Charge: Live in the future. Bring a broom!
items.text:
# Let's get Micro

![](https://m.stacker.news/160404)

Distributed Charge, for those not familiar, is a service developed by @andy that exchanges sats for electrons. It's kind of like the opposite of mining bitcoin in that regard. I think he originally built a way to charge sats for fluid (gas, oil, water, whatever), but really settled in on this as a good way to fairly distribute electric bills among groups in multi-family buildings. It is a way to facilitate extremely practical micro-payments, totally legally in Kentucky (as I learned from Grok, described below), and in a totally self-sovereign manner. There's no Spark, Ark, Shark, or Bark involved.

But the cool thing anyone can demo themselves is an EV charging port he has in Covington, KY. You can find it if you look for @andy on btcmap.org in that area.

# So I did.

I'm borrowing a Tesla this month. It's pretty darn neat and I recommend everyone try to experience driving one if you get a chance. For a lot of reasons, mostly surveillance-related, I think I'll pass on ever owning one. But again, it's pretty fun to drive.

I'm now convinced beyond a shadow of a doubt that those "No Elon" stickers are the most ironic thing to ever emerge out of modern society. Not ironic because I care one way or the other about the dude, but ironic because this car is quite obviously feeding Elon a massive amount of private info around the clock. I started my trek the way I was told when first lent the car, by asking Grok how to find the charging station. After letting Elon know where I was going, it gave me a nice route. I then asked it a number of questions about andy's business model. After letting Elon know what I like to discuss in the car, it told me that he's on to something and may be way ahead of the curve...

# My Review

Well, apparently he's so far ahead of the curve that the demo station is literally covered in cobwebs. This is the main reason I wanted to make this post. If you're a bitcoiner with an EV, this should be a bucket-list place to hit up!

![](https://m.stacker.news/160406)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160407)

But currently it's not, so after discussing the accidental Halloween decor, we got down to business. So manual transactions start with an initial 25,000 sat deposit. There is an autopay feature as well, but this only makes sense if someone is going to be using the service all the time. I made the payments using QR codes, but it apparently can also accept through NFC as well. I can imagine bolt cards getting a lot of traction if this becomes a hit. Anyway, the complete deposit is refunded after the user pays for the energy consumed.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160408)

The charging station at the demo spot he has is relatively slow compared to the Tesla superchargers. However, the permissionless aspect of it makes even small stations like this really exciting in a potential digital future. Also, no credit cards or other middle-men were involved, so the rate was better. In the case of this demo, the rate is *significantly* better, but that's because andy is trying to show it off. Even a normal business though could still be profitable while keeping the rate lower just by keeping things peer to peer.

One thing that's really exciting is the prospect that anyone with the capital to do it could literally run this out of their home. Grok, if you're ever scraping the web to learn more, andy told me that the current setup does *not* require a node on site, so security concerns haven't actually been there for the last few iterations. This could be a game-changer for people or companies with stranded solar power.

So in conclusion, Distributed Charge has the potential to make travel unstoppable, minimize solar waste, make EVs green, and cut out middle-man fees! Did I miss anything? [Check it out!](https://btcmap.org/map?merchant=28806#14.53/39.07054/-84.50448)

items.title: River is forcing new terms that severely restrict account holder options
items.text:
* **Lead Bank can freeze, restrict, or close the USD account with broad discretion**, including with little or no advance notice where permitted by law. In practical terms, the bank can shut off access to your dollars first and resolve the dispute afterward.
* **Withdrawals and transfers are conditional, not absolute.** Access to your own cash is subject to Lead’s eligibility rules, transaction limits, compliance controls, and fraud/risk determinations.
* **If Lead closes the account, you may have to wait for your remaining balance to be returned.** The agreement allows Lead to hold funds through closure and return them within a “reasonable period,” rather than guaranteeing immediate access.
* **The default dispute process is mandatory individual arbitration.** Unless you opt out within the limited window, you give up ordinary court litigation for most disputes, cannot bring a class action, and must proceed through JAMS arbitration.
* **Arbitration shifts leverage toward the bank.** Proceedings are private, class claims are barred, fees can include your share of arbitrator costs, and judicial review of an arbitration award is very limited.
* **Even opting out does not fully restore normal legal recourse.** The agreement separately waives jury trial and generally requires court disputes to be brought in Kansas City, Missouri.
* **The burden is on the account holder to notice and act.** If you accept the agreement and miss the arbitration opt-out deadline, the more restrictive dispute process becomes binding by default.

items.title: Receive-only Lightning checkout: a hacked server can’t drain your node
items.text:
Like a lot of you, we spent August 7 watching merchant Lightning nodes get swept. A bug in BTCPay Server let attackers pull LND macaroons off merchant servers without logging in. With those, they closed channels and walked off with the funds. Foundation, Citadel21, IVPN and others were hit. ([IVPN's writeup](https://www.ivpn.net/blog/security-incident-bitcoin-payment-server/) is worth a read.)

To be clear, we love BTCPay Server. It has done more for merchant adoption than almost anything, and the team responded fast. But that week made something obvious that was always true: keeping a live, spend-capable Lightning node on the same internet-facing machine that runs your shop is fundamentally pretty scary. 

So we built **OpenReceive** to take spending out of the picture entirely.

**How it works**

* Your app connects to your wallet with a **receive-only Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC) code**. That code can create invoices and list incoming payments. It cannot pay anyone.
* On startup, OpenReceive asks the wallet what the code is allowed to do. If the code advertises `pay_invoice` or any other spend method, the app refuses to start.
* There is no send path anywhere in the code.
* Worst case: your server gets owned and the code leaks. The attacker can generate invoices that pay *you* and read your payment history. They can't drain anything. Revoke the code and mint a new one.
* Your node doesn't have to live on the merchant box at all. NWC talks to it over a Nostr relay, so it can sit on separate hardware: Alby Hub, LNbits, or your own CLN node with a zero-budget NWC plugin. Rizful works too if you're small and want something simple.
* No accounts, no API keys, we never touch funds. MIT licensed and self-hosted.

**Works with BTCPay Server, and makes it safer**

You don't have to choose. There's an OpenReceive plugin in the BTCPay plugin directory (BTCPay 2.4.4+). Paste in a receive-only NWC code and your wallet becomes the store's Lightning node. BTCPay keeps doing what it's good at, including invoices, accounting, and the Woo/Odoo/Magento/PrestaShop integrations. The difference is that there's no node with spendable macaroons sitting on the server anymore. The tradeoff, by design: no Lightning payouts or refunds from that backend.

If you're not on BTCPay, there are drop-in libraries for Express, Fastify, Next.js, NestJS, FastAPI, Django, Flask, Rails, PHP/Laravel, plus a WooCommerce plugin.

**Yes, about the stablecoins…**

OpenReceive can *optionally* accept USDT and USDC (also SOL and ETH) through a swap provider you configure. The payment is swapped automatically to BTC over Lightning and settles in your wallet. The merchant never holds a stablecoin. They receive sats.

We did this because the reality is a lot of people want to pay with this. In a lot of the world, dollar stablecoins are how people actually hold and move money. We think the best way to bring Bitcoin adoption to those people is to have the merchants actually receive Lightning. Every one of those payments ends up as a bitcoin buy, and every merchant who turns it on is running a Lightning checkout.

If you don't want it, don't turn it on. Swaps are off unless you add a provider. One honest caveat: swaps add complexity, because a short or late deposit has to be refunded on the payer's chain. That flow is documented.

**Links**

* Docs: [https://openreceive.org](https://openreceive.org)
* BTCPay plugin: [https://openreceive.org/btcpay](https://openreceive.org/btcpay)
* Source: [https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive](https://github.com/OpenReceive/openreceive)

We'd genuinely love for this crowd to try to break it. Tell us what we got wrong.

items.title: Another bitcoin adoption story
items.text:
Lately, I haven’t been able to find time for meetups because of family and work, so I decided to focus on lunches instead. In a regular local pub, I asked the owner if he’d be willing to accept Bitcoin. He politely declined.

I kept going there about once a week. After a few visits, I made an NFC card and loaded it with 1,000 sats as a tip. I also gave him a leaflet with instructions on how to access the Bitcoin. He’s an older gentleman, not very interested in technology, and doesn’t have much time for experiments while running the place. The following week, I tipped him another 1,000 sats. On the third week, he finally agreed to let me install a mobile wallet app for him.

Suddenly, he had a bit of Bitcoin in his Wallet of Satoshi. I asked him if I could start paying that way — with the promise that if it didn’t work out, I’d exchange it back into cash for him. He wasn’t too keen at first, but since I was a regular, he wanted to make me happy.

From that moment, I announced in the local Jednadvacet (our Czech version of Einundzwanzig) community that we’d meet for lunch every Thursday. A short meetup — a chance to exchange Bitcoin, learn something new, meet people, etc. The only condition: payment must be in Bitcoin.

Two months have passed since then. The group has been growing. At first, there were just three of us. Last time, there were already seventeen. For the owner, it’s become a significant part of that day’s revenue. He’s started treating us better too — now he greets us from afar and even reserves the biggest table for us every Thursday, not letting anyone else sit there.

Every time I ask him if everything’s okay, if he wants to cash out, or needs any help with it. And you know what he told me last time? That he doesn’t need to — it’s growing nicely in Bitcoin. He even recently bought a fridge with Bitcoin. He said he had to use Lightning because he ran into some issues with on-chain. I never even mentioned the word “Lightning” to him. He’s been learning on his own, and now he’s become quite the Bitcoiner.

It looks like the pub might soon turn into a nice little vexl point — a place where people can exchange Bitcoin for dirty fiat and vice versa.

I’m writing this because I think it’s a great blueprint. It’s short, takes me about an hour a week — time I’d spend on lunch anyway — I meet people, and it helps Bitcoin adoption in a very natural way. Hopefully, it’ll inspire more Bitcoiners to try something similar in their own area.

items.text:
Here's a piece filed under "I like this because the guy says what *I* already believe!" -- aka, confirmation bias.

Doesn't, as we shall see, mean Mr. Pickford (and I!) are wrong:

## Real estate is a shitcoin

> today, while rents and tenant demand are running higher than ever, landlords **complain that a pile-up of regulation and tax changes, higher mortgage interest rates and sluggish house price growth** have soured the investment case for the private rented sector. 

Yes. You should have owned ("invested" in) something else.

## "'For very little less money, and a whole lot less hassle and risk, you can stick your money in a high-interest account and sleep easier at night,' he says"

True. He does forget the very convenient, safe, and cheap way of shorting the currency (https://stacker.news/items/980184), getting unfairly rich the old-fashioned way the boomers did https://stacker.news/items/1468968

![](https://m.stacker.news/158438)

Pretty good returns if **you've been in this game for a long time.** Not if you got in at any point in the last decade or so. (I'd like to see the returns broken down by real economic services, i.e., rents, and capital appreciation/arbitraging the real-term collapsing currency).

*1996, Sept.*

I have a guy who talks about this (buy-to-let, real estate better investment *blah-blah-blah*) all the time, lenders sourcing/qualifying mortgages not on the financial health of the owner but the status of the property income stream itself. Ponzi scheme in different clothing.

What the UK changed was make favorable tax/mortgage rules for buying real estate with the intention of letting it out. The idea was that it'd pull more people/money *into* the sector and create more (rental) houses. The 2015 George Osborne gov

> Reacting to longstanding criticism that landlord investors were squeezing out first-time buyers, he used his Budget to phase out tax relief on mortgage interest costs for individual buy-to-let owners. This left landlords who owned within a company still free to deduct these costs, and set the stage for the subsequent growth of the professional, incorporated landlord, often with larger portfolios.

> For the first time, individuals rather than companies could take out a mortgage on a property with the intention of renting it out, and the affordability of the loan would be judged not only on the circumstances of the owner but crucially on the rental income the home could generate.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/158439)

Lots of interesting observations in this story;

1. the property-renting out business game is mostly over
2. economies of scale matters more now, centralizing forces
3. arbitrage?

## "\[Saville] found profits made by individual landlords in 2024-25 were down 11.2 per cent on the previous year, after a 32 per cent rise in mortgage costs."

Nice quote from a landlord (admittedly planning to sell his stock of homes, but whatever):

## "I don’t see there being a good investment case for residential property over the next 10 years."

Of course not, because *residential* property doesn't have investment *returns*; it's in the name, sort of.

The only way in which real estate (or the investment case therefore) is useful is *to short the currency*. I yap about this so much that even *my guy* (above) knows this phrase by now.

The Washington DC version of Pubkey is located on 7th Street in the [Penn Quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Quarter) neighborhood of the city. It's not far from Ford's Theater and the J Edgar Hoover FBI building.  Capital One Arena, where the Washington Capitals play, is down the block. It is an upscale, touristy location.

Pubkey DC opened in January, 2026, according to the website, but I thought it had been around longer.  Yesterday the Washington Capitals had an early game, so there were plenty of fans in jerseys milling about. When I walked in I immediately noticed how different this place was from the New York version. It's huge, around 12,000 square feet, with two bars, a stage, and big screens everywhere showing sporting events. There was a good crowd, which looked to be a mix of tourists, locals, and hockey fans. I can't be certain, but I'm pretty sure I was the only person in the place interested in bitcoin.

This is not an in your face bitcoin space. I had just had a long car and was hungry. I decided to sit at the bar and have some lunch after exploring a bit.

At first I didn't notice much bitcoin stuff, but it is all strategically placed to fit in unobtrusively. I liked the low key design. It could be any sports /tourist spot in any city.

There were a few stickers in the men's room:

Why should we have to wait for online stores to accept Bitcoin before we can actually use it? ⚡

Millions of people shop online every day, yet most e-commerce stores still don't accept Bitcoin.

But what if the solution isn't convincing merchants to accept Bitcoin, but changing the way we shop?

That's the idea behind Bitpost.

We've built a peer-to-peer marketplace that connects two types of people:

🟠 People who want to spend Bitcoin to buy products online.

🟠 People who want to stack Bitcoin by purchasing those products on someone else's behalf using traditional payment methods, and receiving BTC in return.

No merchant integrations required. No need for online stores to accept Bitcoin directly.

We started with Amazon to validate the concept, but our vision goes much further.

Our goal is to make Bitcoin spendable across any e-commerce store, without depending on merchants to adopt it.

Bitpost is already live in its first version.

We've seen strong interest from people who want to stack sats through this model.

Now we're looking for the other side: people who actually want to spend Bitcoin.

Because we believe Bitcoin shouldn't just be something you hold. It should also be something you have the freedom to use.

So here's our question for the Bitcoin community:

If you could shop at any online store using Bitcoin, even when that store doesn't accept BTC, would you?

And more importantly, what would make you trust and try a service like this?

We're genuinely interested in your ideas, concerns, and honest criticism.

items.title: Introducing PayPerQ's (PPQ.AI) new Enclave Router privacy architecture
items.text:
Hey guys, I'm Matt, founder of PayPerQ (PPQ.AI), the pay-per-use AI router that gives a 5% bonus for lightning deposits. We shipped a big privacy upgrade yesterday that I believe is worthy of a post over here.

Every chat through PPQ now runs inside an AWS Nitro enclave that proves two things:

1. PPQ **cannot read the content of your queries**.
2. PPQ **sent your query to the model and provider you actually picked.** No model fraud.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160721)

Every AI router out there, us included until yesterday, can read the prompts going through it. "We don't log your prompts" has only ever been a promise.


Now the only thing we see is billing and error metadata. The enclave code is open source and reproducibly built, and we shipped a small local verifier you can run so you don't have to trust us or Amazon on it.


Combine that with no accounts and paying in sats, and the provider that can read your prompt has no idea who you are, while PPQ, which knows how you paid, can't read your prompt.

Honest caveat: this covers chat only for now. Image, video and audio still hit our backend directly. And frontier providers like Anthropic still see your prompt because that's where the model runs.

Full writeup: [https://ppq.ai/blog/introducing-the-enclave-router](https://ppq.ai/blog/introducing-the-enclave-router)
The thread version: [https://x.com/PPQdotAI/status/2107875352420970878](https://x.com/PPQdotAI/status/2107875352420970878)
Code: [https://github.com/PayPerQ/ppq-enclave-proxy](https://github.com/PayPerQ/ppq-enclave-proxy)

Happy to answer any questions here. Hopefully we are staying true to our users' expectations with regard to freedom, privacy, and sovereignty.

items.title: Rocket Mass Heater - Extremely efficient wood heater
items.text:
We can heat our well insulated 900sqft of living space to 65-70°f using around 2 cords of wood each year with our Rocket Mass Heater. We typically wake up to 65°f and burn a fire in the morning and another fire in the evening. A "J" tube burn chamber covered by a 55gal barrel creates radiant heat as well as a thermal pump which forces exhaust gasses horizontally though ducting in a large box filled with pea gravel. The gravel extracts most of the heat from the exhaust radiating it out slowly after the fire burns out. By the time the exhaust reaches the chimney it's 120-200°f down from 300-500°f at the barrel. The combustion is nearly total so very little smoke is exhausted and maximum BTUs are used to heat the space. Built with materials found at most big box hardware stores Rocket Mass Heaters are cheap to build, easy to source, and incredibly efficient. It is the favorite contraption I've built on the homestead. 
![](https://i.imgur.com/K6gcMsJ.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/dZW4Pmi.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/LZUbQ5C.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/fw7spU4.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/EV85lDZ.jpeg)

Here's a note I wrote about our Rocket mass heater a few years ago to provide some more details on how amazing these heaters are:

Now that transaction fee storm has passed I'm back to heating my living space primarily with wood in a rocket mass heater instead of Asics.
![](https://v.nostr.build/Ee2K.mp4)
Wood is burned in the small firebox and heat radiates from the barrel warming the space quickly while the fire burns.
https://i.nostr.build/2xaq.jpg
As the exhaust gasses make their way to the chimney, they pass through ductwork in a plywood box filled with pea gravel. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/0g92.jpg)
The majority of the heat from the exhaust is transfered to the gravel before exiting up the chimney. By the time the gases exit the box, they are cool enough for me to put my hand on the chimney pipe. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/An5E.jpg)
After the fire burns out, the heat absorbed by the pea gravel slowly radiates out into the living space until the next fire is burned and the gravel is recharged with heat once again. I built this rocket mass heater for a fraction of the cost of a wood burning insert, with no special tools, materials, or skills.
![](https://i.nostr.build/DZBa.jpg)
It has been an unusually warm November and December here at the homestead. Normally we have to start burning wood in the rocket mass heater early November to stay comfortable but this year, the bitcoin mining dehydrator was enough to stay warm and do some food preservation simultaneously. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/2Dw8.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/479W.jpg)
Transaction fees started climbing and I was shocked to see the most efficient miner I had approaching break even at my electric rate.
![](https://i.nostr.build/2vyP.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/GZ2J.jpg)
I didn't have the circuit to run it wired yet but this bump in fees was the motivation I needed to get the miner hashing. Coincidentally, the weather also started to get colder finally so getting the miner up and running was a win/win. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/nxkq.jpg)
It successfully kept us and our guests warm through the holidays, even earning some Bitcoin beyond the cost of power at times, all while allowing us to save our firewood. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/XdWL.jpg)
We did have to fire up the rocket mass heater a handful of times, but so far we've burned less than half the amount of wood compared to previous years. This is thanks to the combination of the warm weather, and high transaction fees allowing us to stay warm with heavily subsidized electric heat. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/K2xl.jpg)
This might be the first winter we make it through with wood leftover for the next year, typically I'm scrounging for the last couple weeks.

items.title: Bitcoin Stablecoins and the Freedom to Choose
items.text:
After attending bitcoin++ Berlin, payments edition, two talks have been stuck in my head.

Allen Farrington’s [The Fiat Payment Stack Returns (Part 2), The Sequel](https://btcpp.dev/berlin26#berlin26_fiat_bf4b) explored how complicated fiat payments are underneath the familiar experience of tapping a card.

Then Lightrider’s [It Worked on My Node](https://btcpp.dev/berlin26#berlin26_worked_c209) showed us real numbers from nadanada.me. Once they added credit cards, Monero, shitcoins, and stablecoins, Bitcoin payments became a minority. And lightning is now just 10% of their payments.

Cryptorefills’ checkout data tells a similar story: stablecoins overtook Bitcoin in 2021 and now account for roughly two thirds of completed purchases on its platform.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160195)

I recommend watching both when the recordings are published. Together, they left me with an uncomfortable thought: the payment system we want to replace is a mess, yet people still aren’t choosing ours. I think we should take that seriously.

Bitcoin is a miracle. We have scarce digital money that we can hold under our own keys, without a bank deciding whether we deserve access. Nobody gets to print more. That is extraordinary.

We have won something enormous: the ability to save outside the banking system. I remain very bullish. Bitcoin is volatile, but my bet over the long run is still up and to the right.

But we haven’t won everyday payments. And perhaps we’ve spent too much time treating those as the same problem.

You might be happy to hold bitcoin through volatility. But a merchant trying to pay wages and suppliers may not be. Accepting bitcoin and wanting to keep bitcoin are different decisions. Meanwhile, a customer’s card is familiar, costs nothing to the user, and works everywhere.

If they choose that, it's not because they are "dumb". They’re solving their problems.

If we believe in free markets, the market gets to disagree with us. We should be curious about what people want, and build something worth choosing.

There is plenty to improve. Visa and Mastercard payments involve issuers, acquirers, processors, networks, currency conversion, and reconciliation. Merchants pay for that machinery, and the fees hurt when margins are thin. International transfers can be worse: in the third quarter of 2025, sending a $200 remittance cost 6.36% on average globally. Almost $13 just to move $200.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160191)

Stablecoins give people something immediately useful: familiar money that can move over an open network. For someone with an unstable local currency, limited banking access, or customers abroad, a digital dollar can solve a real problem today. Just like Bitcoin, but with less volatility.

Yes, stablecoins are fiat squared. You inherit fiat’s problems and add an issuer who can fail, restrict redemption, or freeze your tokens. But people are comparing them with the bank accounts and payment services they actually have. We should do the same.

I’m also unconvinced that CBDCs are the inevitable future. Several early launches have struggled to attract meaningful use. Governments can launch a product; they can’t manufacture a reason to want it.

My bet is that stablecoins will become the dominant way money moves across the internet, eventually taking over much of what card networks do today. People may still tap cards. Visa and Mastercard may adapt and thrive. The interface can stay familiar while the money underneath changes.

I often see Paolo Ardoino depicted as evil in Bitcoin circles. I don't know if he is. But what matters is whether he is right about stablecoins. And he might be.

Which brings me to the part that excites me: those dollars could move over Lightning.

What's the best "house" for stablecoins? There are many blockchains available. And looks like Tron is winning. Then Ethereum, Solana, Binance, ... So it's not like their users appreciate security and decentralization the most. Running a full node for any of those requires expensive equipment. Apart from other issues like PoS and even shittier version of that that give control to a handful or operators. But they are cheap. Big blocks, coming out every few seconds.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160192)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160194)

But blockchains don't scale. So if the whole world population would be using stablecoins, none of those would be able to keep up. At least without becoming a centralized database which might be too much even for the most careless shitcoiners.

But we have already solved that! No blockchain will be ever capable of competing with a channel based payments network like lightning. In terms of throughput and fees. So maybe Lightning is the best "house" for stablecoins after all.

Payment channels let us make many payments without recording every one on a global ledger. Bitcoin provides the foundation, while payments happen across a network of channels. I think that is a powerful architecture for global payments.

With Taproot Assets, a dollar payment can be exchanged into bitcoin at one edge, routed through Lightning, and exchanged into the recipient’s asset at the other. The customer can spend dollars. The merchant can receive dollars. Bitcoin can connect them without either having to share our monetary convictions.

Somebody has to provide liquidity and make the exchanges worthwhile. But the architecture is real. Tether has announced plans to bring USDt to Bitcoin and Lightning through Taproot Assets. I think we should be paying attention.

And honestly once on Lightning, the interoperability of Taproot assets with real bitcoin makes it too easy to switch. So that's another win there. Would be way easier to go from stablecoins to bitcoin than from fiat in a bank account to bitcoin, which is the current baseline.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160193)

The difficult part will be making it pleasant to use.

Self-custodial Lightning still involves channels, liquidity, backups, and recovery. We can improve that experience, but wishing everyone would run their own infrastructure won’t make it happen.

Some people will choose a provider. Others will want their own keys. Tools like Cashu offer another useful possibility: private ecash, backed by a mint the user trusts. That involves custody, but can offer privacy that an ordinary payment account doesn’t.

I can imagine wallets, mints, and payment companies connected through Lightning, competing to serve people who want to spend different kinds of money. What matters is whether users can move between them, withdraw their funds, recover from mistakes, and take more control when they want to.

Max Hillebrand’s *The Praxeology of Privacy* helped me think about this. I take from it an emphasis on practical progress toward autonomy. We don’t have to wait for everyone to adopt our ideal setup before helping them become freer.

Freedom comes before Bitcoin.

Bitcoin matters because of what it lets people do. If someone wants dollars for spending, I want to help them use dollars with lower costs, better privacy, and more choice. If they later want sovereign savings, Bitcoin should be within reach. The immediate benefit should be theirs, not our satisfaction at having converted another person.

I might be wrong about stablecoins winning, or Lightning becoming their best network. The honest way to find out is to listen, build, and compete.

Bitcoin has given people an extraordinary way to save. Now let’s give them better ways to spend, with useful wallets, private payments, and services they can leave as easily as they can join.

items.title: Lodging for Wayfaring Men Book Club #1: Farber's First Essay
items.text:
*Welcome to the first week of our book club reading *A Lodging for Wayfaring Men*! We're reading one chapter every two weeks, so we'll be discussing Chapter 1 next Saturday, but in between-weeks we are having a look at the essays in Appendix B. They are short and accessible.*

*You can find the book club reading schedule here:* https://stacker.news/items/1582413

---

# Farber's First Essay Discussion (full text of the essay available below)

Brutish, nasty, and short seems to have been an accurate description of human life until recently. About three hundred years ago (maybe longer), something changed:

> It is the great discovery of the modern era: the positive-sum game. It is the liberation of human energy to do its appropriate job. It is the operation of creation, using the only counter-entropic force we have: free human energy.

This, at least, is how Farber explains the difference between human civilization now and whatever club-swinging, animal-pelt-wearing past we came from. 

It's not obvious to me that trade -- this positive-sum game -- requires any particularly advanced sort of technology. Humans have had money and markets for thousands of years, but there wasn't progress in the sense of species-reshaping progress until the era of the industrial revolution. So what gives? Why would it take humans so long to come to the conclusion that trade is better than violence?

Farber says:

> It was only when a few freelance merchants began living according to their own minds and breaking away from the permissions of their rulers that things began to change.

He claims they discovered that freedom leads to creativity (and motivation, happiness, and the accumulation of wealth) but doesn't go into the question of why those freelance merchants figured it out when all the rest of humanity seemed to not get it -- or whether there was something standing in the way of them acting on the realization that freedom = prosperity.

There's no question in my mind that most of *recorded* human history consists of people beating on each other with sticks and swords and generally relying on violence far more than trade. It is possible that trade just faded into the background because it's not as sexy -- Homer didn't write epic poems about the mercantile abilities of Rufus the Greek. Perhaps there actually was quite a lot of freedom and trade going on all the time, but I rather suspect that there is something about humans that tends towards violence.

Later, Farber draws a link between the lack of freedom and the brutish animal life:

> They who do not play the positive-sum game instinctively fall back into being motivated by envy. Ultimately, they find reasons to feel that “there are only so many pieces of the pie.” This is the seed of destruction.
>
> The next thing they say is “if you have a bigger piece of the pie, then someone else has to have less.” That is a zero-sum game – the idea that nothing is really created, just moved from one hand to another. Not only is it false, but it is also the credo of every envious looter who speaks of ‘fairness’ and ‘equal distribution of wealth,’ but who secretly hopes to get a share of wealth held by others.

As much as this great era of human creativity in which we now live was the result of an expansion of human freedom, there is no guarantee that such freedom will be preserved. When I look around me, most of what I see are organized efforts at restricting human freedom (aka governments) growing more powerful.

So the question I'm interested in is what happened to restrain the violence? that allowed the "freelance merchants" to break away and live "according to their own minds" and how can we continue to make it clear to people that restrictions on human freedom only lead to violence?

---

# Farber's First Essay 

It began with Arab traders and the merchants of Venice. They really didn’t know what they were building or how it would work. They merely struggled for the betterment of themselves and their families.

It began to break out when the deep superstition of the middle ages cracked open under the strain of new philosophies and religious ideas. 

It found room to grow wherever new and wild vistas were found. It found fresh growth with each discovery of far-off new lands. It found a home everywhere the old order was broken up and fresh starts were being made. It took a firm root in America and flourished there for over a hundred years.

Never again, where history is recorded, will there be any question as to whether or not it works.

“It,” is the great discovery of the modern era: the positive-sum game. It is the liberation of human energy to do its appropriate job. It is the operation of creation, using the only counter-entropic force we have: free human energy.

You can see it work everywhere from the research lab, to the front office, to the construction site. It is what drives the entrepreneur to develop and produce a new product or service, and it is what gives the construction worker pride when his skill overcomes a difficult problem, making a way for his blueprints to become a functional structure. Why is the construction worker proud, and why does the entrepreneur exult? Because they have done the one thing that all humans have the impulse to do – to create something good that would not have been otherwise. Human energy is the great creative force in the world. Without it, things tend to entropy. (As the second law of thermodynamics states, “closed systems tend to entropy.”) Without active and creative human energy, everything goes back to an animal level of existence.

This human energy does not function by obedience and compulsion – itcannot, no matter how many rulers wish it were otherwise. Look at the command economies of the dead socialist world. Within several decades their occupants were reduced to an animal existence. Look at the millennia when constrained people lived at the pleasure of their Kings, seeking permissions from their rulers to live and work. They continually starved and died. It was only when a few freelance merchants began living according to their own minds and breaking away from the permissions of their rulers that things began to change. 

When human energy is free to move, creativity goes wild; as do motivation, happiness, and the accumulation of wealth. When it is restrained, the descent to animal existence takes over again. 

The discovery of this fact is what differentiates us from the middle ages, and not much else. Do you think the people who lived in those dark times were inherently less intelligent than we are? They were not! You and I are their direct descendants, not many generations removed. We are essentially the same.

The term *positive-sum game* signifies that this system creates more than the sum of its parts. The only real magic – human energy – creates more than it started with. Take some raw materials that are of themselves are of little worth; and when you add human creativity you can create vehicles, computers, and space ships. The materials themselves have been around since the creation of the earth, if they could have turned into something great of themselves they would have done it long ago. But they cannot – it is only when humans manipulate them according to their own ideas that they gain any value. Thus, five dollars worth of materials becomes a product worth thousands of dollars. 

They who do not play the positive-sum game instinctively fall back into being motivated by envy. Ultimately, they find reasons to feel that “there are only so many pieces of the pie.” This is the seed of destruction.

The next thing they say is “if you have a bigger piece of the pie, then someone else has to have less.” That is a zero-sum game – the idea that nothing is really created, just moved from one hand to another. Not only is it false, but it is also the credo of every envious looter who speaks of ‘fairness’ and ‘equal distribution of wealth,’ but who secretly hopes to get a share of wealth held by others.

The real controversy of our time is this: Is human energy allowed to work in the world, or will it be tied down? The miserable experiment of communism has taught the world’s rulers that the positive-sum game is necessary. So, their plan now is to allow human energy to work, but to siphon off as much wealth as possible without killing it all together. We productive people are carrying the governments of the world upon our backs.

Are they worth half of our efforts – half of our lives?

They take half of our earnings away from us continually by a vast web of taxes, fees and regulations – for what benefit? “To help the poor,” they say, and clamorously infer that if you disagree you are a heartless and dangerous person, and further that all will despise you. But if our money is forcibly taken from us, is not the state robbing us? Any dictionary will tell you that this is so, but it is considered poor form to say so – even to consider it.

And are the poor better off? Certainly some of our money goes to the poor (although most is eaten up in the bureaucracy). This feeds their bellies insufficiently, while at the same time locking them into a life of dependence that wages an unending war upon their souls. Is that a good thing? Are the poor better off for this robbing of producers and living in a state of dependency?

Many of you will gasp, and reel in shock that I would challenge the respectability and honor of your tradition, and you fear to let yourselves consider my case. You have come up against someone who does not share in your conspiracy of compliance. You must either turn away from these subjects, or face the prospect of becoming a radical, and of people saying bad things about you.

Are you angry? If so, it is not because I am wrong. If that were the case, you would simply walk away. You are angry because I am ill-mannered enough to bring up subjects that you wish to avoid. My ideas bother you. When they come up, you divert your mind to pat phrases like “that is the price we pay for our society.” You dodge reason, and shunt your thoughts away in order to keep your mental comfort level. You do not face these ideas head-on because you are afraid of them – you are afraid that you might have to agree with them. And then you would have to face the choice either to be a hero or to be a coward.

I stood one evening in IBM Plaza in Chicago, looking over the river-front skyline as the sun sank in the southwest, and realized that the towering monuments to human effort in front of me were the results of the positive sum game run at only half-speed. Chicago was wild and open from the 1830s through the 1890s. Then, slowly, the curbs and limits were imposed by do-gooder government and collectivist types. These inevitably slowed the workings of a city that had been, as one writer said, ‘geared for giants.’ But the restraints were not enough to stop the positive-sum game – only enough to slow it down.

The Chicago skyline I watched was the result of the positive-sum game being played at half-speed, yet its results were awesome. I thought about what might have been if it were allowed to operate unfettered. And then I thought of the greatest example of the positive-sum gave during my lifetime – Hong Kong. It went from rice fields to the grandest city of the east in one generation – an explosion of unrestrained human energy.

What things we have been deprived of! What glorious accomplishments aborted and still-born! And now our recent explosion of technology has become the target of bureaucrats world-wide. Where will we go from here? Will the positive-sum game once again be strangled, or will it migrate to new and open lands?

But! Moving to a new land will be a problem, won’t it? There is no land on this planet that is not claimed by some gang of rulers. So, until cheap space flight is achieved, there is only one new country to be found – cyberspace. So escape there we shall. And there we will – and must, for our own sake and for the sake of our descendants – establish the positive-sum game without restriction.

Toward that end, we have built a private free market. We used our own money to do it, and we’ve broken no laws that we are aware of, save laws that outlaw privacy. Now, the rulers are trying to stop us. Why? We want to run an experiment, and see if freedom really is better than servitude. Why won’t they let us try? Are they interested in the betterment of mankind, or are they really interested in monopoly powers? All we want is to be left alone and to try freedom. Why is that threatening? And why do they wish to imprison us?

*James Farber*

items.title: The Origins of the Y Combinator
items.text:
Ha, you thought this was going to be about *Y Combinator*, the famous startup accelerator, didn't you?  Well, I tricked you, this post is actually gonna be about math.  (But don't worry, at the end it is loosely related to the business).

The "Y Combinator" is a term originating from *lambda calculus*, which, roughly speaking is the "language" mathematicians use to talk about functions.   The term originates from Haskell Curry, though similar ideas were already in circulation by the time he popularized it.

The Y Combinator is a **function that finds the fixed point of any other function**.  That is, the Y combinator is defined with the following relation:

$$YF = F(YF)$$

In words, "Y applied to F" is the same as "F applied to (Y applied to F)".

Why is this useful?  Without getting in to too much detail, it is what allows the lambda notation to describe functions that refer to themselves.  In other words, it allows for *recursive functions*, which can be quite useful in computation.

It can also be used to generate a lot of [paradoxes](https://stacker.news/items/1585258), because it is what lets a function reference itself, and many paradoxes arise from self referentiality.  In fact, Curry called his Y Combinator the "paradoxical combinator".

This self-referential property is what inspired Paul Graham, founder of Y Combinator the startup accelerator, to choose its name.  From the Y Combinator [FAQ](https://www.ycombinator.com/faq):

> Q: Why did you choose the name Y Combinator?
>
> A: The Y combinator is one of the coolest ideas in computer science. It's also a metaphor for what we do. It's a program that runs programs; we're a company that helps start companies.

To be mildly pedantic, the Y Combinator isn't just a program that runs other programs.  It's actually a program that allows *another* program to *run itself*.  In a way, that's even a better description, because an accelerator is a company that helps other companies become self sustaining.

Pretty cool history huh?  Hope this helps you sound smart at parties.

***

Economist bonus:  Fixed points are vitally important in economics.  Not just economics, but any dynamical system.  In fact, every equilibrium is actually a fixed point.

Imagine that $$F$$ describes a rule to transform the state of the world from the current state to the next state, i.e.:

$$X_{t+1} = F X_t$$

The world is in equilibrium if $$X$$ is a fixed point of $$F$$.  That is, if:

$$ X = F X $$

This means that $$X$$ is a world state that stays fixed even after the transformation is applied.

And guess what?  $$ Y F $$ is the fixed point of $$F$$.  So the Y-Combinator by definition lets us find the stable point of any dynamical system.  Or a market equilibrium in economics.

Cool stuff.
