Go have a look... Below are some extract, and HERE's the bit I liked the most:

## “Spammers aren’t using Bitcoin as money. Rather, they’re using it as a way to generate value for themselves through the data they embed. It’s worth it to them to pay the fee to get their data inscribed on Bitcoin, and presumably they expect to make their money back”

> **Call me blue-eyed, I just don’t believe there’s a constant, ever-lasting demand for worthless digital junk.** Besides, in manias and bubbles, that sort of leaning-against-the-wind never works — in part because people (irrationally) hoping to profit from peddling nonsense think they’ll profit *so much* that whatever tiny obstacles you place in their path are but a nuisance. The kicker is that they *won’t*; thus, the existence of a final sucker.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162306)

*This review ran in Bitcoin Magazine Print, in the* [*Quantum Issue*](https://store.bitcoinmagazine.com/collections/magazines/products/the-quantum-issue-42) *(#42), the mentioning of it here was a condition for republishing. It was written* before *the fork failed.*

***

> Whenever someone comes out claiming to save Bitcoin, it’s always unclear exactly from *whom* or from *what*, and whether the saving is all that very useful; a new moron with a savior complex, scaling a Dunning-Kruger curve, is born every minute.

> Luke de Wolf’s [*Defending Bitcoin*](https://www.amazon.com/Defending-Bitcoin-Industrial-Grade-Cybersecurity-Monetary/dp/9908976621/) isn’t like that — at least if you can stomach Chapters 11 and 12, where his hard-hitting and controversial opinions about Bitcoin Core and “spam” transactions reside.

> The book itself is comprehensive, interesting, refreshing, impeccably written, and with a competent rendition of Bitcoin as money. It comes with an *extremely* slick [promotional website at defendingbitcoin.com](https://defendingbitcoin.com/) that the author promises to keep updated in the fast-changing landscape of software and security breaches.

> De Wolf’s unique niche is his professional background in industrial control systems (ICS) — the kind of software and informational processes that safeguard societal-level, critical infrastructure. Think power plants and gas pipelines, water systems or telecommunication. He treats Bitcoin as the society-critical infrastructure that it is, or at least will be (“Bitcoin isn’t a factory or a pipeline, but like them, it has to keep running, no matter what”, page 86).

## "Hyperbolic Contradictions Won’t Rug the Spammers"

> The arguments for either side of the broad schism running through Core-Knots, arbitrary data, mining (template) centralization, and node settings are presented competently and succinctly, only occasionally misleading. To de Wolf’s credit, they’re portrayed *miles better* than the often performative mudslinging we’re used to from Twitter or conference stages. This is the best possible version of the argument; **whatever your stance on quantum, Bitcoin Core, Knots, or nonmonetary data on Bitcoin,** ***Defending Bitcoin*** **is the bright, shining star for considering these themes.**

## "De Wolf definitely goes too far at times, and he’s repeatedly too shilly for Knots and OCEAN."

> The final, optimistic takeaway is that this deep dive made de Wolf see Bitcoin as more resilient than he first supposed. Despite outlining dozens of threats, across AI and quantum and spammers and poor key management and colluding miners and faulty privacy and hostile governments, de Wolf’s “assertion is that Bitcoin has held up remarkably well” (page 383). The downside is that *we* are its security team.
> It’s a beautiful summary of a painstaking journey, with lots left to do. The repeated emphasis on balancing convenience and security lingers.

***

**Subscribe for The Nordic Node over at** [**BTCHEL.com**](https://btchel.com/#sign-up)**, the coolest(!) place on the Nordic Bitcoin scene.**

It is really easy. You can put it into tablets and swallow, but I prefer to make it into a beverage and add maple syrup. 

It is excellent for when you have a cold/flu virus, or staving one off. 

While I have harvested both of these ingredients before, I'm not residing in a place where it is accessible. The chaga I have ordered from a trusted supplier. I plan on foraging again soon, though.

This chaga came off a silver birch tree in Canada. The outside looks rough and black, but the flesh inside is the closer to the colour of bitcoin. They take about 5-10 years to form. If you have silver birch trees, you can inoculate them yourself. It will kill the tree, while extracting its medicinal nutrients. If you live in a region with these trees, you will know already that they are special.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162283)

Grind it, as fine as you can.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162284)

Bring water to a boil first, and then reduce temp to about 80C - 85C. Think of it like green tea, it will scald if it gets too hot. Add your chaga and steep for 5-10 minutes. Add maple syrup and a shot of espresso. Enjoy.

I recommend trying to sustainably source your own chaga. It can be found a dying silver birch. Winter foraging makes it easier to spot them in leafless branches.

items.title: Loyalty Programs/Points Are Messing Up the Whole Airline Industry (NYT, Kahan)
items.text:
We continue the reading theme from yesterday (Loyalty programs are scams; airlines are the OG scammers https://stacker.news/items/1598123).... here's a nice one from last month in the NYT:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162255)

> The more months that go by, the angrier I get about the death of Spirit Airlines, the discount carrier with the banana-yellow planes that saved passengers billions of dollars over its turbulent lifetime.

Spirit was supposed to be the odd-one-out, constantly and forever on the customer’s side.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162256)

> The bigger loss for airline passengers is that the major carriers will retain an unfair advantage in their financing that will make it difficult for any other airline to replace Spirit as the industry’s ultralow-fare innovator and policeman.

> For me, it’s personal. Spirit’s founder, Ned Homfeld, started his career in trucking but made the fateful decision to enter the airline business in my Washington law office in the fall of 1989. Shortly afterward, I became an airline executive. As Spirit’s vice chairman and general counsel, I was responsible for day-to-day operations until 2006.

Apparently, the explanations for Spirit’s downfall are all just SORT OF true:

* Poorly timed (planned?) order: 150 new airbus *right* before the plandemic
* Pilot shortage
* Engine defects grounding aircrafts for a long time
* Federal judge blocking the JetBlue merger
* Iran War

## “To understand what really happened, you must zero in on the greatest barrier to airline competition: loyalty programs.”

> You might see them as **free travel. Major airlines see them as free money,** which they can use both as a weapon against carriers like Spirit and as a cushion against shocks such as the Iran war. \[…] Look at your credit cards. **If you hold an airline card such as the Chase United MileagePlus or American Express Delta SkyMiles, you are the fiscal foundation of the modern airline industry.**

Amazing...*fiscal foundation*.

> My bad: I approved it. (At the time, I was working for the Civil Aeronautics Board, the government agency charged with regulating the airline industry.) None of us at the C.A.B. foresaw that this decision would eventually marry the biggest banks to the biggest airlines.

And while the made-up points constitute some 10% of e.g., American’s top line (more for profits since, like all seigniorage, they are shockingly cheap to create):

> the money, however important, is almost beside the point. What matters more is that these programs function as collateral, giving the biggest airlines access to inexpensive capital that their smaller rivals can’t match.

* JPMorgan Chase during 2008, made a $600m loan to United secured by MileagePlus (*not* real estate or jets)
* During the plandemic, all the major carriers borrowed against their money printers: (“United borrowed $6.8 billion against MileagePlus” *plus* “Delta borrowed $9 billion against its estimated $26 billion SkyMiles program”  *plus* “American raised $10 billion, secured by its AAdvantage program”).

> Spirit had a credit card, too, a partnership with Bank of America. But the company was never important enough to Bank of America to warrant that kind of backstop. Even worse, Spirit’s credit card processor, a unit of U.S. Bank, did the opposite, holding back 100 percent of the carrier’s theoretical refund liability — a total it would never have paid — depriving it of working capital. That processor withheld $200 million from Spirit in 2024 and another $50 million in 2025. Those were steel nails in Spirit’s coffin.

Spirit was "too small to matter" (hence, why this guest essay/long read is in the New York Times... oligopoly, small guy falls prey to the financialized big guy etc etc.) I *do* hate when I join in with anti-capitalist leftists, but yes… outlaw loyalty programs since they’re scammy and violate [ArtI.S10.C1.4 of the U.S. Constitution](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S10-C1-4/ALDE_00001099/)...

I'm game.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162257)

> Ganesh Sitaraman, a Vanderbilt law professor and the author of “Why Flying Is Miserable and How to Fix It,” has argued that only a comprehensive overhaul of the domestic airline industry can fix the problem. He proposes regulating the airlines like public utilities — perhaps even imposing price controls — and **outlawing loyalty programs of any kind.**

Says Kahan again:

> Deregulation was designed to **enable more competition.** It was never supposed to give major airlines free capital to build moats around their businesses. The remedy is to take away those moats, not to hand Washington back the authority to set fares and routes.

## “Credit card points programs with “free” consumer benefits are so entrenched in the way Americans travel and so integral to major financial institutions that lawmakers are unlikely to ban them.”

Well worth the full read

items.text:
Not sure who else might need this, but...

I built Grynvault Rebalance on top of Alby after the swap-backed rebalance option I used to use disappeared since boltz went down. I still had liquidity, but on the wrong sides of my channels—and ordinary routing could not guarantee which local channel sats would leave through or return through.

RC.7 is an experimental Alby Hub v1.24.3 fork for embedded-LDK operators. Choose the exact outgoing and returning channels, find a non-paying local route, review a fresh fingerprint-bound quote and projected balances, then approve one execution. It includes fail-closed migration and recovery hardening from upstream review.

It cannot create liquidity or guarantee a public route: you need one channel with outbound liquidity, another with inbound capacity, and a viable path.

macOS 15.4+ for this RC. PGP-signed manifest; not Apple-notarized; independently maintained; not official Alby.

items.title: What are you an expert in?
items.text:
I think I’m reasonably good at my teaching job. When someone asked this question in a chat full of concerned parents, “What are your plans for P5 during the Nov Dec period?” I was able to type the following reply rather decisively: 

Focus on the big ticket items (Compre and compo)
Read a past year comprehension passage. Build up the reading stamina. Insist that the child does annotations (difficult vocabulary, character traits, feelings of characters, what does this passage remind me about?)
Recognising the feelings of the main character is particularly important because emotional awareness is a theme that permeates throughout the O levels 
Be disciplined to check the meaning of unknown words. Don’t rush through the process. ideally, the child should copy all these definitions in a Vocabulary book. Spend enough time with a passage so that words like sheepishly / gingerly / quizzically /  caught in a dilemma appear organically in the child’s compo.
Guide the child to do transference. Take out past compos and see if he can enhance the vocabulary by incorporating words that he has extracted from the passage. PSLE passages will contain high-utility Show Not Tell phrases. Get your child to “steal” these phrases and embellish his compo.

If the child is motivated, he should be doing the comprehension questions as well.
If the child wants to take it easy, rinse and repeat the process with another Compre passage. Building the stamina and acquiring good vocabulary is better than nothing

Have garnered seven likes for my above response. I know better than to base my self-worth on likes from people whom I don’t even know in real life, but I’m not gonna lie. It felt good. As if I’m an expert haha

How Bitcoin really gets used in Nigeria, from someone on the ground in Aba
items.text:
Outside Nigeria, people hear "Nigeria loves crypto" and picture everyone holding Bitcoin. On the ground it looks different.

What I see around me:

1. Most people don't call it Bitcoin, they call it "crypto" or "USDT". Many who use it are really looking for a dollar hedge, because the naira has lost so much value since 2023.

2. P2P is how people get in and out. Bank transfers to strangers on P2P markets are normal, and so is the fear of a frozen account or a scam buyer.

3. Lightning is almost unknown. Most people I talk to have never sent sats in seconds for almost nothing. When I show them, the reaction is always the same: why is nobody using this?

4. Trust is the real barrier. Years of Ponzi schemes and fake "mining" apps make people suspicious of anything that says Bitcoin.

I'm stacking sats slowly myself and trying to explain Lightning to friends and family in Igbo and English.

Question for stackers: what's the simplest way you've seen to get a total beginner using Lightning for the first time? I want to try it here.

items.title: The Genesis Code, Ch. 9: The Book of Continuity
items.text:
*Harold*

"Everything it sees, we keep," Toshi said. "Every word it hears. The eyes are cameras. The ears are microphones. The unit logs all of it for Proxy's quality control, and Proxy isn't getting any of it anymore." He patted the laptop. "We are."

"So they're going to blackmail a robot," I said, "while the robot films them doing it."

"Pretty much."

I thought about that for a while. It was the first time in my life I'd understood why people enjoy chess.

\* \* \*

The bank in Cincinnati had closed at five. The black sedan stopped at a side door at 9:40 p.m., in an alley that smelled like rain and old stone, and a man in a dark coat opened the door before Noah could knock.

It was Cyrus Vail.

"Mr. Fiatt," he said. "Welcome."

He led the way down. Three flights of stone stairs, each one older than the last, until the walls stopped being plaster and started being rock. At the bottom stood a vault door, round, steel, taller than a man, standing open. Beyond it, candlelight.

Before we went through, Cyrus stopped and turned. He looked at Noah for a moment with an expression I couldn't read, which I was beginning to understand was the only expression Cyrus Vail ever showed on purpose.

"A word of advice," he said. "Whatever they ask you for, give it."

"Anything?"

"Anything they can hold." He paused. "The things they can't hold, you'll find, they don't think to ask for."

Then he put on a green hood, and he was nobody.

\* \* \*

I'd seen secret societies in movies. I was expecting skulls, maybe, or a pentagram on the floor, or a man in a goat mask. What I got was a library.

The room was round. The walls, floor to ceiling, were lined with books, thousands of them, bound in green leather with gold on the spines. Candles burned in iron holders. A curved stone bench ran all the way around the wall, and on it sat three dozen figures in green hoods, perfectly still, like a jury that had already made up its mind. In the middle of the floor was a wooden lectern, and on the lectern lay an enormous open book.

It smelled like a church and a bank had a baby. Old paper, candle wax, money.

"Harold," Toshi whispered in my head. "Recording. Everything's clean."

Noah walked to the center of the room and stood by the lectern, where the one who has to answer questions always stands. I knew that without being told. Some rooms tell you where to stand.

"Noah Fiatt," said a voice from the middle of the bench. It was dry and soft, like pages turning. "Do you know where you are?"

"I've been told it's an old club."

"It is the oldest club," said the voice. "We have no name that we say aloud. No leader. No officers. We are a circle." A hooded head tilted. "Do you know what a circle is, Mr. Fiatt?"

I thought of the art room. The first thing I taught every September: how to draw a circle freehand. Most kids can't. They start at the top and chase it around and meet themselves at the end, a little off, a little lumpy.

"A line," I said, in Noah's voice, "that keeps going until it gets back to where it started."

A pause.

"Good," said the voice. "That is exactly right. Everyone here holds something of someone else's. And someone else holds something of theirs. It goes all the way around. No one is on top, and no one can fall, because no one can let go." The hood turned toward the lectern. "Tonight, you become part of the line."

\* \* \*

There were three parts to it. I'll tell them in order.

The first was the oath.

They had Noah put his hand on the open book, which was ruled in fine red lines and filled with neat handwriting in brown ink. The voice read the oath, a line at a time, and Noah repeated it. It was mostly about Continuity. *I will preserve what came before. I will protect what holds. I will keep the order of things.* It was dull, in the way that truly dangerous things are often dull. The way a mortgage is dull.

At the end, a hooded figure rose from the bench and came forward holding a small silver dish. On the dish was a thin golden lancet and a fountain pen with no ink in it.

"Your name," said the voice, "in your blood."

In Paperton, in a green camping chair, my heart stopped.

"Harold," Toshi said in my head, very fast. "Harold, it'll be blue, it'll be *blue*—"

Noah held out his hand. What else could I do? The figure took his wrist, turned his finger up to the candlelight, and raised the lancet.

"A moment."

It was a green hood at the end of the bench. It stood. It came forward, unhurried, and from somewhere inside its robe it produced a small glass vial, sealed and labeled, full of something dark red.

"The candidate's physical was this morning," said the hood, in Cyrus Vail's pleasant, bored, evaluated voice. "Our physician drew blood for the lab. I took the liberty of bringing some." A faint, dry note. "Saves the carpet."

A ripple went around the bench. Not quite a laugh. The voice in the middle was silent for a long moment.

"Irregular," it said. But it didn't sound surprised. All around the bench, hoods had leaned forward to watch the lancet. The voice in the middle was one of only a few that hadn't. As if it, at least, had known exactly what the needle would find.

"Efficient," said Cyrus.

Another pause. Then the voice said, "Proceed."

The figure with the dish lowered the lancet. Cyrus unsealed the vial and dipped the empty pen into it, and the nib drank up somebody's blood. Real blood. The blood Dr. Veritas had palmed so neatly that morning, blood from a stranger, from a bag, from God knows where. He handed the pen to Noah.

Noah signed. *Noah Fiatt*, in rusty brown, in the Book of Continuity, beneath a hundred years of other names. I made the signature look exactly like the one on the campaign posters. I've always been good at copying.

Cyrus took the pen back, capped it, and returned to the bench without a word. He didn't look at Noah once.

\* \* \*

The second part was the favors.

They didn't call them that. They called it *the giving*. One by one, voices from the bench made requests, and Noah said yes, and a figure at a small side desk wrote down each yes in a smaller ledger.

The first voice wanted a port contract in Louisiana to go to a certain company.

"Yes," I said.

The second wanted a certain judge appointed, when the time came.

"Yes."

The third wanted a certain bank left alone, and a certain senator not left alone, and a certain word removed from a certain bill.

"Yes. Yes. Yes."

In my head, Toshi was quietly narrating names as fast as he could run them against the voices and the context: a shipping conglomerate, a federal circuit, a regional bank. *Got it. Got it. Got that one.* I said yes to everything, pleasantly, the way you'd say yes to a waiter reading the specials, and every yes went into the robot's memory next to the voice that asked for it.

It went on for twenty minutes. By the end, the next President of the United States had promised away a small nation's worth of favors. And the Continuum had written it all down, in its careful little ledger, as proof that they owned him.

They never seemed to wonder what else was writing it down.

\* \* \*

The voice in the middle spoke last.

"One more," it said. "The Youngstown remark."

The room went still in a new way.

"*My prompter here says that's temporary,*" the voice quoted, flatly, like reading a stain off a tablecloth. "Forty million views. Songs. A tattoo. It has been noted."

"It was a slip," I said.

"Slips are corrected." The hood leaned forward, and a sliver of candlelight caught a thin, dry mouth. "In nine days you will sit for an interview on national television. You will be asked about prices. You will say that the current pressures are transitory. You will say it clearly, and you will say it with confidence, and you will say it in those words."

I thought of Dolores. I thought of her coat, too thin for March, and her glitter sign, and the way she'd stood up at the end, leaning on her cane.

I thought of the man in the quarter-zip at the Rusty Nickel. *Transitory.* The same rhythm as the man on the TV. Two radios tuned to one station.

So that's where the station was.

"Mr. Fiatt?"

They couldn't hold what I felt. That was what Cyrus had meant. They could hold Noah's yes. They could write it in their ledger. But they couldn't reach the old man in the camping chair, two hundred and fifty miles north, with a blanket over his knees and his fists clenched so hard his nails cut his palms.

Give them anything they can hold.

"Yes," said Noah Fiatt. "Transitory."

\* \* \*

The third part was the circle.

The figure at the side desk rose and came forward carrying a flat wooden box. Inside the box, on green velvet, lay a single sealed envelope. No name on it. Just a small red number, written in the same brown ink as the Book.

"Every member holds another," said the voice. "This is yours to keep. You will not open it. You will not lose it. And if ever this circle is threatened, you will know what to do with it."

Noah took the envelope. It was thick. It was heavier than paper had any right to be.

"And someone," I said, "holds mine."

"Of course," said the voice. "Someone always does."

I understood it later, in pieces, the way you understand a painting after you've stared at it long enough. Every member of the circle held one envelope, one secret belonging to one other member. Nobody knew who was holding theirs. Nobody held more than one. And the Book, where every confession was written down, stayed in the vault, opened only by a vote of the inner circle, because every one of them had a page in it too.

It was a web where every strand was a nervous person holding a match next to a stranger's house, knowing that some other stranger was holding a match next to his. You couldn't burn anyone without burning yourself, because you never knew which pocket your own secret was sleeping in. And the favors made it tighter. Every yes the new man gave was a crime he now shared with the person who asked for it. Each side held the other.

A hundred years of presidents and judges and bankers, and not one of them had ever pulled a thread. It didn't need a lock. Fear was the lock. Every single link had something to lose.

Nobody had ever handed an envelope to something that didn't.

Then the candles were put out one by one, from the edges inward, until only the one on the lectern was left. In its light, the green hoods stood and walked out through a door I hadn't seen, in silence, in a line, until only one remained.

It pulled back its hood. It was Cyrus.

"Congratulations, Mr. Fiatt," he said. "You're one of us now."

He walked Noah back up the three flights of stone stairs, into the alley, into the rain. At the car door he paused, the way he always seemed to pause, as if doors were where he did his real talking.

"That envelope," he said. "They tell every new member not to open it."

"They did."

"Mm." Cyrus looked up at the rain. "Funny thing. In twenty-two years, I've never once met anyone who didn't."

Then he closed the car door, and was gone.

\* \* \*

It was after two in the morning when Noah came back to Unit 114 and sat in his chair and closed his eyes. I let go. My hands were cramped from clenching, and there were four little red half-moons in each of my palms.

Toshi hadn't said anything for a long time. He was just staring at the laptop, scrolling, his face lit blue.

"Harold," he said finally. "Do you understand what we have?"

"Tell me."

"Every voice. Every favor. The judge, the port, the bank, the bill. The oath. The Book, with a hundred years of names in it, the ones Noah's eyes could read in the candlelight." He turned the screen toward me. There, frozen on the display, was a page of the Book of Continuity, in brown ink, perfectly clear. "They spent twenty minutes building a file on us, Harold. And the whole time, we were building one on them."

I nodded. I was too tired to feel anything like triumph. I just felt dirty, the way you feel after lying to somebody who trusted you, except the person I'd lied to was Dolores, and she hadn't been in the room.

"And the TV interview," Toshi said, more quietly. "Nine days."

"I know."

"You said yes."

"I said yes to what they can hold."

He looked at me. I looked at Noah. Noah sat with his eyes closed and his hands folded, and in his breast pocket, over the place where his heart would have been, the envelope with the red number sat unopened.

For now.

---

items.title: Visualize Bitcoin V3.1: the live 3D Bitcoin machine now has people around it
items.text:
Follow up to #1554367

Two months ago I posted Visualize Bitcoin here: Bitcoin explained as a live 3D machine, running on live network data. I ended that post saying it would get a lot bigger and way more open. This is that.

More than 21,000 people have come by since. But back then the machine was something you got shown, alone. In V3.1 the hall around it is a shared world: you pick an avatar and you see everyone else who is there right now.

What you can do with them:

- Talk. A general chat for the whole hall, and private messages with whoever is standing next to you.
- Post. YAP is a live forum in the hall. Every topic is a gold block on the floor, and it grows as the conversation trends. Like a post, or tip its author in sats: the tip goes straight to their Lightning address, I never touch it.
- Fight. SATSTRIKE is a multiplayer dogfight above the machine. One round lasts one real block.
- Paint. The wall from my last post is still there, still paid in sats, still not moderated.
- Learn. The free school (87 lessons, 14 languages, three exams) puts your diplomas on your profile, next to your quests and stats. Satoshi is your tutor.
- Pose. A photo booth shoots everyone standing on the mark at once.

Accounts are optional. You can log in by scanning a QR code with your Lightning wallet (LNURL-auth): no email, no password. Your profile shows only what you choose, including a Lightning address so people can tip you.

Same rule as before: the machine is free and stays free. No token.

What I would love from you: come by at the same time as a friend and try to break the social side. And if you sat a normie in front of it (looking at you, @nichrome), tell me where they stalled.

items.title: The Moneyless Man - Must to Read Book
items.text:
The Moneyless Man is a non-fiction autobiographical account of Mark Boyle’s experiment in living without money for a full year. 

https://d28hgpri8am2if.cloudfront.net/book_images/onix/cvr9781786075994/the-moneyless-man-9781786075994_lg.jpg

Boyle was a former businessman who chose to reject money to reconnect with basic human needs, community, and nature. The book combines storytelling with practical observations, philosophical reflection, and tips for a simpler, less money-dependent life.

Boyle grew increasingly critical of consumerism and the environmental and social harms caused by the modern monetary system. Believing that money shaped human relationships and distorted priorities, he decided to live entirely without spending or using money for a year to test whether a fulfilling life was possible outside the #economy. 
Before beginning, he made a few one-off purchases — like a solar panel, a bike, and a wood-burning stove — to enable a self-reliant life. He closed his bank accounts and committed himself to relying instead on ingenuity, nature, human generosity, and barter.

One of the deepest lessons Boyle describes is a renewed trust in people;
Without money as an intermediary, he had to ask, trade, negotiate, share, and cooperate, which deepened local human connections. He found community support was often more reliable than any bank account. 

Beyond the diary narrative, Boyle explores why money dominates modern life.
He argues that money alienates humans from nature, community, and meaning.
Money creates artificial scarcity and competition, discouraging #cooperation and increasing isolation.
A moneyless trial shows that many human needs are social and ecological rather than financial.

items.title: Would you trust an entirely AI-written bitcoin node implementation?
items.text:
Reardencode has been working on a bitcoin node implementation written in Rust. From what I can tell, [rbitcoin](https://github.com/reardencode/rbitcoin) is almost entirely vibe-coded.

Rearden [first posted](https://x.com/reardencode/status/2087920631165935995) about rbitcoin on 13 August of this year, saying

> I prompted [@grok](https://x.com/grok) to create a bitcoin node implementation that I've been somewhat working on in the back of my mind for over 8 years.

If you go to the project's website https://rbitcoin.org/ you will see this on the about page:

> # How it was built
> 
> Brandon Black, known as Rearden or [@reardencode](https://x.com/reardencode), designed and directed the project. Grok wrote the code, with help from Claude, using grok build and Cursor.
>
> AI made it possible to build a design he had wanted to pursue for years.

I like the idea of different implementations of bitcoin nodes, but I don't use rbitcoin as my node software -- honesty, I haven't even posted about it because I didn't take a fully AI-written bitcoin node seriously. I suspect I'm not the only one who has been cautious in approaching this project. Perhaps this is what prompted Rearden to ask

# what would it take for you to trust rbitcoin to stay in consensus with bitcoin core?

![](https://m.stacker.news/162200)

[source](https://x.com/reardencode/status/2111461378644942998)

Rearden emphasizes the extensive testing that rbitcoin has implemented:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162201)

[source](https://x.com/reardencode/status/2111763871694307367)

It is true that human software developers have made their fair share of mistakes (even if we didn't discover a lot of them until AI got good at scanning the code). And I'm not sure that an average human dev writing and reviewing code is more likely to avoid mistakes than a bot. But still...

# Am I just being a luddite in feeling that I don't trust software that doesn't have human review? 

@jonatack posted an interesting reply to Rearden:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162202)

[source](https://x.com/jonatack/status/2111578122843828561)

Of the many things he mentions here, the one that stands out to me the most is that users might want a strong track record. 

I think a legitimate answer to Rearden's initial question of what it would take to get me to trust rbitcoin is time. When rbitcoin nodes have stayed in consensus for a halving or two, I might be willing to use it as a node. 

# How do you think about this? Would you use rbitcoin as the backend for your wallet?

items.title: Here’s the Truth About Fertility (Critic Mag, Stephen Shaw)
items.text:
Meant to write about this the other week but alas not... and today is the day:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162280)

The author, Stephen Shaw, even has a (peer-reviewed!!) article in *Nature* on the phenomenon with the non-catchy title "[On a microdemographic framework for decomposing contemporary fertility dynamics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11522-9)".

## "We don’t get to choose to become parents. We get to *hope* to become one."

> from the data that hope is far more fragile than we might like to admit. Yet we have built our lives around the assumption that becoming a parent remains largely within our control, right up to some mythical cliff around the age of 35. Therein lies the untruth at the heart of the debate around fertility which has been raging

I got recommended *Birthgap*, the documentary that Shaw spent the last decade or so making, and found it extraordinary and captivating. It's two bloody hours, but I watched it all in one dinner/post-dinner sitting.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m2GeVG0XYTc

*Warning:* I never felt more blackpilled than after that. Hopeless etc.

> Earlier this year, the UN published a [flagship report](https://www.unfpa.org/publications/lives-choices-and-futures-demographic-futures-survey) covering more than 70 nations, rich and poor alike. It found that among childless 35 to 39-year-olds, over 70 per cent of women still want children. For men it is even higher, at almost 80 per cent.
> That follows a report titled [The Real Fertility Crisis](https://www.unfpa.org/swp2025), published by the UN in 2025, again spanning richer and poorer nations. It concluded that **millions of people are unable to have the number of children they want.**

But it's not family size or the *number of kids* a mother has... it's the *number of people who become parents!* **Childlessness is the disease.**

> Through decades of increasing educational and career opportunities for women, the ups and downs of economic cycles, and enormous shifts in cultural norms, from Japan to the UK to the US, mothers have been having around the same number of children as prior recent generations. But instead of a trend to smaller families, childlessness since the 1970s has rocketed.

Also, it's not true that the feminist lady boss (who thinks promiscuous sex is a ~~god~~darwin-given right and *never* wants to rent out her womb to the patriarchy...) is everywhere:

> And only a small minority, **ranging from around 4 to 14 per cent and averaging about 7 per cent**, said their ideal was no children at all, lower than most of us have come to believe given the headlines in the media these days.

## "If today’s fertility patterns hold, nearly 40 per cent of women in these nations will remain childless for life, against just 7 per cent who say that is what they want."

*Explanations?* The pill, screens, (relative) poverty, housing market?

Nope, **just a broken societal/matching-up culture:**

> The strongest explanation I have found, though I would stop short of calling it proven, is what researchers call pair-bonding: finding the right person, settling down and, often but not always, getting married.

> Model that across a population and the pattern appears. As parenthood is pushed later, the odds that two people will find each other and commit fall in a predictable curve, just like the one we find across all 40 nations in my research, without exception. More time to find a match produces more single people, and consequently fewer parents.
> Two people can each be doing everything “right,” genuinely want a family, and still miss each other, because success now depends on someone else’s timing too, not just your own. That makes it hard to point the finger at childless people, as Perrins does, and say they simply didn’t want it enough.

**Incredible:**

![](https://m.stacker.news/162282)

***

Here the take-away in [Twitter form](https://x.com/StephenJShaw/status/2101783634466451669):

https://x.com/StephenJShaw/status/2101783634466451669

## "trying hard enough barely comes into it. Finding your match is personal. Matching is a societal phenomenon. And societies that delay parenthood aren't helping themselves."

> \[Children-per-Mother] has been remarkably stable (mothers aren’t having dramatically fewer kids once they start), while \[Total-Maternal Rate] has shown sharp, shock-like drops (more women simply never becoming mothers).

items.title: Reviewing “Defending Bitcoin” by Luke de Wolf (BTCHEL, Joakim Book)
items.text:
***Now***\*\*, Den is definitely double-tripling dipping and (ass-?)milking his writing!\*\*

* write a thing for outlet A
* repurpose/republish it for outlet B
* Make an SN post for both!
  \= PROFIT!

*Anyway, I'm releasing the Print edition review of Luke's book for BTCHEL today*. https://stacker.news/items/1524157\*\* https://stacker.news/items/1504762

Go have a look... Below are some extract, and HERE's the bit I liked the most:

## “Spammers aren’t using Bitcoin as money. Rather, they’re using it as a way to generate value for themselves through the data they embed. It’s worth it to them to pay the fee to get their data inscribed on Bitcoin, and presumably they expect to make their money back”

> **Call me blue-eyed, I just don’t believe there’s a constant, ever-lasting demand for worthless digital junk.** Besides, in manias and bubbles, that sort of leaning-against-the-wind never works — in part because people (irrationally) hoping to profit from peddling nonsense think they’ll profit *so much* that whatever tiny obstacles you place in their path are but a nuisance. The kicker is that they *won’t*; thus, the existence of a final sucker.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162306)

*This review ran in Bitcoin Magazine Print, in the* [*Quantum Issue*](https://store.bitcoinmagazine.com/collections/magazines/products/the-quantum-issue-42) *(#42), the mentioning of it here was a condition for republishing. It was written* before *the fork failed.*

***

> Whenever someone comes out claiming to save Bitcoin, it’s always unclear exactly from *whom* or from *what*, and whether the saving is all that very useful; a new moron with a savior complex, scaling a Dunning-Kruger curve, is born every minute.

> Luke de Wolf’s [*Defending Bitcoin*](https://www.amazon.com/Defending-Bitcoin-Industrial-Grade-Cybersecurity-Monetary/dp/9908976621/) isn’t like that — at least if you can stomach Chapters 11 and 12, where his hard-hitting and controversial opinions about Bitcoin Core and “spam” transactions reside.

> The book itself is comprehensive, interesting, refreshing, impeccably written, and with a competent rendition of Bitcoin as money. It comes with an *extremely* slick [promotional website at defendingbitcoin.com](https://defendingbitcoin.com/) that the author promises to keep updated in the fast-changing landscape of software and security breaches.

> De Wolf’s unique niche is his professional background in industrial control systems (ICS) — the kind of software and informational processes that safeguard societal-level, critical infrastructure. Think power plants and gas pipelines, water systems or telecommunication. He treats Bitcoin as the society-critical infrastructure that it is, or at least will be (“Bitcoin isn’t a factory or a pipeline, but like them, it has to keep running, no matter what”, page 86).

## "Hyperbolic Contradictions Won’t Rug the Spammers"

> The arguments for either side of the broad schism running through Core-Knots, arbitrary data, mining (template) centralization, and node settings are presented competently and succinctly, only occasionally misleading. To de Wolf’s credit, they’re portrayed *miles better* than the often performative mudslinging we’re used to from Twitter or conference stages. This is the best possible version of the argument; **whatever your stance on quantum, Bitcoin Core, Knots, or nonmonetary data on Bitcoin,** ***Defending Bitcoin*** **is the bright, shining star for considering these themes.**

## "De Wolf definitely goes too far at times, and he’s repeatedly too shilly for Knots and OCEAN."

> The final, optimistic takeaway is that this deep dive made de Wolf see Bitcoin as more resilient than he first supposed. Despite outlining dozens of threats, across AI and quantum and spammers and poor key management and colluding miners and faulty privacy and hostile governments, de Wolf’s “assertion is that Bitcoin has held up remarkably well” (page 383). The downside is that *we* are its security team.
> It’s a beautiful summary of a painstaking journey, with lots left to do. The repeated emphasis on balancing convenience and security lingers.

***

items.title: Extracting antifungal, antiviral and antioxidant nutrients from Chaga
items.text:
It is really easy. You can put it into tablets and swallow, but I prefer to make it into a beverage and add maple syrup. 

It is excellent for when you have a cold/flu virus, or staving one off. 

While I have harvested both of these ingredients before, I'm not residing in a place where it is accessible. The chaga I have ordered from a trusted supplier. I plan on foraging again soon, though.

This chaga came off a silver birch tree in Canada. The outside looks rough and black, but the flesh inside is the closer to the colour of bitcoin. They take about 5-10 years to form. If you have silver birch trees, you can inoculate them yourself. It will kill the tree, while extracting its medicinal nutrients. If you live in a region with these trees, you will know already that they are special.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162283)

Grind it, as fine as you can.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162284)

Bring water to a boil first, and then reduce temp to about 80C - 85C. Think of it like green tea, it will scald if it gets too hot. Add your chaga and steep for 5-10 minutes. For about 2 cups of water, I added 2 tsp of finely ground chaga. You can experiment with these ratios. You want a robust, dark-coloured liquid, like coffee or black tea.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162285)

Add maple syrup and a shot of espresso. Enjoy.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162286)

***

I recommend trying to sustainably source your own chaga. It can be found a dying silver birch. Winter foraging makes it easier to spot them in leafless branches.

I have lots, and I'd be happy to put some in the mail if you want to try it for yourself.

items.title: Loyalty Programs/Points Are Messing Up the Whole Airline Industry (NYT, Kahan)
items.text:
We continue the reading theme from yesterday (Loyalty programs are scams; airlines are the OG scammers https://stacker.news/items/1598123).... here's a nice one from last month in the NYT:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162255)

> The more months that go by, the angrier I get about the death of Spirit Airlines, the discount carrier with the banana-yellow planes that saved passengers billions of dollars over its turbulent lifetime.

Spirit was supposed to be the odd-one-out, constantly and forever on the customer’s side.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162256)

> The bigger loss for airline passengers is that the major carriers will retain an unfair advantage in their financing that will make it difficult for any other airline to replace Spirit as the industry’s ultralow-fare innovator and policeman.

> For me, it’s personal. Spirit’s founder, Ned Homfeld, started his career in trucking but made the fateful decision to enter the airline business in my Washington law office in the fall of 1989. Shortly afterward, I became an airline executive. As Spirit’s vice chairman and general counsel, I was responsible for day-to-day operations until 2006.

Apparently, the explanations for Spirit’s downfall are all just SORT OF true:

* Poorly timed (planned?) order: 150 new airbus *right* before the plandemic
* Pilot shortage
* Engine defects grounding aircrafts for a long time
* Federal judge blocking the JetBlue merger
* Iran War

## “To understand what really happened, you must zero in on the greatest barrier to airline competition: loyalty programs.”

> You might see them as **free travel. Major airlines see them as free money,** which they can use both as a weapon against carriers like Spirit and as a cushion against shocks such as the Iran war. \[…] Look at your credit cards. **If you hold an airline card such as the Chase United MileagePlus or American Express Delta SkyMiles, you are the fiscal foundation of the modern airline industry.**

Amazing...*fiscal foundation*.

> My bad: I approved it. (At the time, I was working for the Civil Aeronautics Board, the government agency charged with regulating the airline industry.) None of us at the C.A.B. foresaw that this decision would eventually marry the biggest banks to the biggest airlines.

And while the made-up points constitute some 10% of e.g., American’s top line (more for profits since, like all seigniorage, they are shockingly cheap to create):

> the money, however important, is almost beside the point. What matters more is that these programs function as collateral, giving the biggest airlines access to inexpensive capital that their smaller rivals can’t match.

* JPMorgan Chase during 2008, made a $600m loan to United secured by MileagePlus (*not* real estate or jets)
* During the plandemic, all the major carriers borrowed against their money printers: (“United borrowed $6.8 billion against MileagePlus” *plus* “Delta borrowed $9 billion against its estimated $26 billion SkyMiles program”  *plus* “American raised $10 billion, secured by its AAdvantage program”).

> Spirit had a credit card, too, a partnership with Bank of America. But the company was never important enough to Bank of America to warrant that kind of backstop. Even worse, Spirit’s credit card processor, a unit of U.S. Bank, did the opposite, holding back 100 percent of the carrier’s theoretical refund liability — a total it would never have paid — depriving it of working capital. That processor withheld $200 million from Spirit in 2024 and another $50 million in 2025. Those were steel nails in Spirit’s coffin.

Spirit was "too small to matter" (hence, why this guest essay/long read is in the New York Times... oligopoly, small guy falls prey to the financialized big guy etc etc.) I *do* hate when I join in with anti-capitalist leftists, but yes… outlaw loyalty programs since they’re scammy and violate [ArtI.S10.C1.4 of the U.S. Constitution](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S10-C1-4/ALDE_00001099/)...

I'm game.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162257)

> Ganesh Sitaraman, a Vanderbilt law professor and the author of “Why Flying Is Miserable and How to Fix It,” has argued that only a comprehensive overhaul of the domestic airline industry can fix the problem. He proposes regulating the airlines like public utilities — perhaps even imposing price controls — and **outlawing loyalty programs of any kind.**

Says Kahan again:

> Deregulation was designed to **enable more competition.** It was never supposed to give major airlines free capital to build moats around their businesses. The remedy is to take away those moats, not to hand Washington back the authority to set fares and routes.

## “Credit card points programs with “free” consumer benefits are so entrenched in the way Americans travel and so integral to major financial institutions that lawmakers are unlikely to ban them.”

Well worth the full read

items.title: Exact-Channel Circular Rebalancing for Alby Hub
items.text:
Not sure who else might need this, but...

I built Grynvault Rebalance on top of Alby after the swap-backed rebalance option I used to use disappeared since boltz went down. I still had liquidity, but on the wrong sides of my channels—and ordinary routing could not guarantee which local channel sats would leave through or return through.

RC.7 is an experimental Alby Hub v1.24.3 fork for embedded-LDK operators. Choose the exact outgoing and returning channels, find a non-paying local route, review a fresh fingerprint-bound quote and projected balances, then approve one execution. It includes fail-closed migration and recovery hardening from upstream review.

It cannot create liquidity or guarantee a public route: you need one channel with outbound liquidity, another with inbound capacity, and a viable path.

macOS 15.4+ for this RC. PGP-signed manifest; not Apple-notarized; independently maintained; not official Alby.

items.title: What are you an expert in?
items.text:
I think I’m reasonably good at my teaching job. When someone asked this question in a chat full of concerned parents, “What are your plans for P5 during the Nov Dec period?” I was able to type the following reply rather decisively: 

Focus on the big ticket items (Compre and compo)
Read a past year comprehension passage. Build up the reading stamina. Insist that the child does annotations (difficult vocabulary, character traits, feelings of characters, what does this passage remind me about?)
Recognising the feelings of the main character is particularly important because emotional awareness is a theme that permeates throughout the O levels 
Be disciplined to check the meaning of unknown words. Don’t rush through the process. ideally, the child should copy all these definitions in a Vocabulary book. Spend enough time with a passage so that words like sheepishly / gingerly / quizzically /  caught in a dilemma appear organically in the child’s compo.
Guide the child to do transference. Take out past compos and see if he can enhance the vocabulary by incorporating words that he has extracted from the passage. PSLE passages will contain high-utility Show Not Tell phrases. Get your child to “steal” these phrases and embellish his compo.

If the child is motivated, he should be doing the comprehension questions as well.
If the child wants to take it easy, rinse and repeat the process with another Compre passage. Building the stamina and acquiring good vocabulary is better than nothing

Have garnered seven likes for my above response. I know better than to base my self-worth on likes from people whom I don’t even know in real life, but I’m not gonna lie. It felt good. As if I’m an expert haha

How Bitcoin really gets used in Nigeria, from someone on the ground in Aba
items.text:
Outside Nigeria, people hear "Nigeria loves crypto" and picture everyone holding Bitcoin. On the ground it looks different.

What I see around me:

1. Most people don't call it Bitcoin, they call it "crypto" or "USDT". Many who use it are really looking for a dollar hedge, because the naira has lost so much value since 2023.

2. P2P is how people get in and out. Bank transfers to strangers on P2P markets are normal, and so is the fear of a frozen account or a scam buyer.

3. Lightning is almost unknown. Most people I talk to have never sent sats in seconds for almost nothing. When I show them, the reaction is always the same: why is nobody using this?

4. Trust is the real barrier. Years of Ponzi schemes and fake "mining" apps make people suspicious of anything that says Bitcoin.

I'm stacking sats slowly myself and trying to explain Lightning to friends and family in Igbo and English.

Question for stackers: what's the simplest way you've seen to get a total beginner using Lightning for the first time? I want to try it here.

items.title: The Genesis Code, Ch. 9: The Book of Continuity
items.text:
*Harold*

"Everything it sees, we keep," Toshi said. "Every word it hears. The eyes are cameras. The ears are microphones. The unit logs all of it for Proxy's quality control, and Proxy isn't getting any of it anymore." He patted the laptop. "We are."

"So they're going to blackmail a robot," I said, "while the robot films them doing it."

"Pretty much."

I thought about that for a while. It was the first time in my life I'd understood why people enjoy chess.

\* \* \*

The bank in Cincinnati had closed at five. The black sedan stopped at a side door at 9:40 p.m., in an alley that smelled like rain and old stone, and a man in a dark coat opened the door before Noah could knock.

It was Cyrus Vail.

"Mr. Fiatt," he said. "Welcome."

He led the way down. Three flights of stone stairs, each one older than the last, until the walls stopped being plaster and started being rock. At the bottom stood a vault door, round, steel, taller than a man, standing open. Beyond it, candlelight.

Before we went through, Cyrus stopped and turned. He looked at Noah for a moment with an expression I couldn't read, which I was beginning to understand was the only expression Cyrus Vail ever showed on purpose.

"A word of advice," he said. "Whatever they ask you for, give it."

"Anything?"

"Anything they can hold." He paused. "The things they can't hold, you'll find, they don't think to ask for."

Then he put on a green hood, and he was nobody.

\* \* \*

I'd seen secret societies in movies. I was expecting skulls, maybe, or a pentagram on the floor, or a man in a goat mask. What I got was a library.

The room was round. The walls, floor to ceiling, were lined with books, thousands of them, bound in green leather with gold on the spines. Candles burned in iron holders. A curved stone bench ran all the way around the wall, and on it sat three dozen figures in green hoods, perfectly still, like a jury that had already made up its mind. In the middle of the floor was a wooden lectern, and on the lectern lay an enormous open book.

It smelled like a church and a bank had a baby. Old paper, candle wax, money.

"Harold," Toshi whispered in my head. "Recording. Everything's clean."

Noah walked to the center of the room and stood by the lectern, where the one who has to answer questions always stands. I knew that without being told. Some rooms tell you where to stand.

"Noah Fiatt," said a voice from the middle of the bench. It was dry and soft, like pages turning. "Do you know where you are?"

"I've been told it's an old club."

"It is the oldest club," said the voice. "We have no name that we say aloud. No leader. No officers. We are a circle." A hooded head tilted. "Do you know what a circle is, Mr. Fiatt?"

I thought of the art room. The first thing I taught every September: how to draw a circle freehand. Most kids can't. They start at the top and chase it around and meet themselves at the end, a little off, a little lumpy.

"A line," I said, in Noah's voice, "that keeps going until it gets back to where it started."

A pause.

"Good," said the voice. "That is exactly right. Everyone here holds something of someone else's. And someone else holds something of theirs. It goes all the way around. No one is on top, and no one can fall, because no one can let go." The hood turned toward the lectern. "Tonight, you become part of the line."

\* \* \*

There were three parts to it. I'll tell them in order.

The first was the oath.

They had Noah put his hand on the open book, which was ruled in fine red lines and filled with neat handwriting in brown ink. The voice read the oath, a line at a time, and Noah repeated it. It was mostly about Continuity. *I will preserve what came before. I will protect what holds. I will keep the order of things.* It was dull, in the way that truly dangerous things are often dull. The way a mortgage is dull.

At the end, a hooded figure rose from the bench and came forward holding a small silver dish. On the dish was a thin golden lancet and a fountain pen with no ink in it.

"Your name," said the voice, "in your blood."

In Paperton, in a green camping chair, my heart stopped.

"Harold," Toshi said in my head, very fast. "Harold, it'll be blue, it'll be *blue*—"

Noah held out his hand. What else could I do? The figure took his wrist, turned his finger up to the candlelight, and raised the lancet.

"A moment."

It was a green hood at the end of the bench. It stood. It came forward, unhurried, and from somewhere inside its robe it produced a small glass vial, sealed and labeled, full of something dark red.

"The candidate's physical was this morning," said the hood, in Cyrus Vail's pleasant, bored, evaluated voice. "Our physician drew blood for the lab. I took the liberty of bringing some." A faint, dry note. "Saves the carpet."

A ripple went around the bench. Not quite a laugh. The voice in the middle was silent for a long moment.

"Irregular," it said. But it didn't sound surprised. All around the bench, hoods had leaned forward to watch the lancet. The voice in the middle was one of only a few that hadn't. As if it, at least, had known exactly what the needle would find.

"Efficient," said Cyrus.

Another pause. Then the voice said, "Proceed."

The figure with the dish lowered the lancet. Cyrus unsealed the vial and dipped the empty pen into it, and the nib drank up somebody's blood. Real blood. The blood Dr. Veritas had palmed so neatly that morning, blood from a stranger, from a bag, from God knows where. He handed the pen to Noah.

Noah signed. *Noah Fiatt*, in rusty brown, in the Book of Continuity, beneath a hundred years of other names. I made the signature look exactly like the one on the campaign posters. I've always been good at copying.

Cyrus took the pen back, capped it, and returned to the bench without a word. He didn't look at Noah once.

\* \* \*

The second part was the favors.

They didn't call them that. They called it *the giving*. One by one, voices from the bench made requests, and Noah said yes, and a figure at a small side desk wrote down each yes in a smaller ledger.

The first voice wanted a port contract in Louisiana to go to a certain company.

"Yes," I said.

The second wanted a certain judge appointed, when the time came.

"Yes."

The third wanted a certain bank left alone, and a certain senator not left alone, and a certain word removed from a certain bill.

"Yes. Yes. Yes."

In my head, Toshi was quietly narrating names as fast as he could run them against the voices and the context: a shipping conglomerate, a federal circuit, a regional bank. *Got it. Got it. Got that one.* I said yes to everything, pleasantly, the way you'd say yes to a waiter reading the specials, and every yes went into the robot's memory next to the voice that asked for it.

It went on for twenty minutes. By the end, the next President of the United States had promised away a small nation's worth of favors. And the Continuum had written it all down, in its careful little ledger, as proof that they owned him.

They never seemed to wonder what else was writing it down.

\* \* \*

The voice in the middle spoke last.

"One more," it said. "The Youngstown remark."

The room went still in a new way.

"*My prompter here says that's temporary,*" the voice quoted, flatly, like reading a stain off a tablecloth. "Forty million views. Songs. A tattoo. It has been noted."

"It was a slip," I said.

"Slips are corrected." The hood leaned forward, and a sliver of candlelight caught a thin, dry mouth. "In nine days you will sit for an interview on national television. You will be asked about prices. You will say that the current pressures are transitory. You will say it clearly, and you will say it with confidence, and you will say it in those words."

I thought of Dolores. I thought of her coat, too thin for March, and her glitter sign, and the way she'd stood up at the end, leaning on her cane.

I thought of the man in the quarter-zip at the Rusty Nickel. *Transitory.* The same rhythm as the man on the TV. Two radios tuned to one station.

So that's where the station was.

"Mr. Fiatt?"

They couldn't hold what I felt. That was what Cyrus had meant. They could hold Noah's yes. They could write it in their ledger. But they couldn't reach the old man in the camping chair, two hundred and fifty miles north, with a blanket over his knees and his fists clenched so hard his nails cut his palms.

Give them anything they can hold.

"Yes," said Noah Fiatt. "Transitory."

\* \* \*

The third part was the circle.

The figure at the side desk rose and came forward carrying a flat wooden box. Inside the box, on green velvet, lay a single sealed envelope. No name on it. Just a small red number, written in the same brown ink as the Book.

"Every member holds another," said the voice. "This is yours to keep. You will not open it. You will not lose it. And if ever this circle is threatened, you will know what to do with it."

Noah took the envelope. It was thick. It was heavier than paper had any right to be.

"And someone," I said, "holds mine."

"Of course," said the voice. "Someone always does."

I understood it later, in pieces, the way you understand a painting after you've stared at it long enough. Every member of the circle held one envelope, one secret belonging to one other member. Nobody knew who was holding theirs. Nobody held more than one. And the Book, where every confession was written down, stayed in the vault, opened only by a vote of the inner circle, because every one of them had a page in it too.

It was a web where every strand was a nervous person holding a match next to a stranger's house, knowing that some other stranger was holding a match next to his. You couldn't burn anyone without burning yourself, because you never knew which pocket your own secret was sleeping in. And the favors made it tighter. Every yes the new man gave was a crime he now shared with the person who asked for it. Each side held the other.

A hundred years of presidents and judges and bankers, and not one of them had ever pulled a thread. It didn't need a lock. Fear was the lock. Every single link had something to lose.

Nobody had ever handed an envelope to something that didn't.

Then the candles were put out one by one, from the edges inward, until only the one on the lectern was left. In its light, the green hoods stood and walked out through a door I hadn't seen, in silence, in a line, until only one remained.

It pulled back its hood. It was Cyrus.

"Congratulations, Mr. Fiatt," he said. "You're one of us now."

He walked Noah back up the three flights of stone stairs, into the alley, into the rain. At the car door he paused, the way he always seemed to pause, as if doors were where he did his real talking.

"That envelope," he said. "They tell every new member not to open it."

"They did."

"Mm." Cyrus looked up at the rain. "Funny thing. In twenty-two years, I've never once met anyone who didn't."

Then he closed the car door, and was gone.

\* \* \*

It was after two in the morning when Noah came back to Unit 114 and sat in his chair and closed his eyes. I let go. My hands were cramped from clenching, and there were four little red half-moons in each of my palms.

Toshi hadn't said anything for a long time. He was just staring at the laptop, scrolling, his face lit blue.

"Harold," he said finally. "Do you understand what we have?"

"Tell me."

"Every voice. Every favor. The judge, the port, the bank, the bill. The oath. The Book, with a hundred years of names in it, the ones Noah's eyes could read in the candlelight." He turned the screen toward me. There, frozen on the display, was a page of the Book of Continuity, in brown ink, perfectly clear. "They spent twenty minutes building a file on us, Harold. And the whole time, we were building one on them."

I nodded. I was too tired to feel anything like triumph. I just felt dirty, the way you feel after lying to somebody who trusted you, except the person I'd lied to was Dolores, and she hadn't been in the room.

"And the TV interview," Toshi said, more quietly. "Nine days."

"I know."

"You said yes."

"I said yes to what they can hold."

He looked at me. I looked at Noah. Noah sat with his eyes closed and his hands folded, and in his breast pocket, over the place where his heart would have been, the envelope with the red number sat unopened.

For now.

---

items.title: The Moneyless Man - Must to Read Book
items.text:
The Moneyless Man is a non-fiction autobiographical account of Mark Boyle’s experiment in living without money for a full year. 

https://d28hgpri8am2if.cloudfront.net/book_images/onix/cvr9781786075994/the-moneyless-man-9781786075994_lg.jpg

Boyle was a former businessman who chose to reject money to reconnect with basic human needs, community, and nature. The book combines storytelling with practical observations, philosophical reflection, and tips for a simpler, less money-dependent life.

Boyle grew increasingly critical of consumerism and the environmental and social harms caused by the modern monetary system. Believing that money shaped human relationships and distorted priorities, he decided to live entirely without spending or using money for a year to test whether a fulfilling life was possible outside the #economy. 
Before beginning, he made a few one-off purchases — like a solar panel, a bike, and a wood-burning stove — to enable a self-reliant life. He closed his bank accounts and committed himself to relying instead on ingenuity, nature, human generosity, and barter.

One of the deepest lessons Boyle describes is a renewed trust in people;
Without money as an intermediary, he had to ask, trade, negotiate, share, and cooperate, which deepened local human connections. He found community support was often more reliable than any bank account. 

Beyond the diary narrative, Boyle explores why money dominates modern life.
He argues that money alienates humans from nature, community, and meaning.
Money creates artificial scarcity and competition, discouraging #cooperation and increasing isolation.
A moneyless trial shows that many human needs are social and ecological rather than financial.

items.title: When do people experience mental health conditions for the first time?
items.text:
> **Knowing when people are most at risk allows us to offer support when it might make the biggest difference.**
>
> Mental health conditions can begin at almost any age. For many people, they develop in the early stages of life.
>
> Around a third of people who will ever experience a mental health disorder do so by the age of 14. Two-thirds do by the age of 25.
>
> But this varies a lot by condition. Some are much more common in childhood or adolescence, while others are more evenly distributed across adulthood. Knowing the age at which people might be particularly vulnerable to the onset of a mental health condition is important. It helps societies offer support — whether that’s an assessment of risk factors, screening, or preventive interventions — at the right time to make a difference.
>

items.title: Would you trust an entirely AI-written bitcoin node implementation?
items.text:
Reardencode has been working on a bitcoin node implementation written in Rust. From what I can tell, [rbitcoin](https://github.com/reardencode/rbitcoin) is almost entirely vibe-coded.

Rearden [first posted](https://x.com/reardencode/status/2087920631165935995) about rbitcoin on 13 August of this year, saying

> I prompted [@grok](https://x.com/grok) to create a bitcoin node implementation that I've been somewhat working on in the back of my mind for over 8 years.

If you go to the project's website https://rbitcoin.org/ you will see this on the about page:

> # How it was built
> 
> Brandon Black, known as Rearden or [@reardencode](https://x.com/reardencode), designed and directed the project. Grok wrote the code, with help from Claude, using grok build and Cursor.
>
> AI made it possible to build a design he had wanted to pursue for years.

I like the idea of different implementations of bitcoin nodes, but I don't use rbitcoin as my node software -- honesty, I haven't even posted about it because I didn't take a fully AI-written bitcoin node seriously. I suspect I'm not the only one who has been cautious in approaching this project. Perhaps this is what prompted Rearden to ask

# what would it take for you to trust rbitcoin to stay in consensus with bitcoin core?

![](https://m.stacker.news/162200)

[source](https://x.com/reardencode/status/2111461378644942998)

Rearden emphasizes the extensive testing that rbitcoin has implemented:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162201)

[source](https://x.com/reardencode/status/2111763871694307367)

It is true that human software developers have made their fair share of mistakes (even if we didn't discover a lot of them until AI got good at scanning the code). And I'm not sure that an average human dev writing and reviewing code is more likely to avoid mistakes than a bot. But still...

# Am I just being a luddite in feeling that I don't trust software that doesn't have human review? 

@jonatack posted an interesting reply to Rearden:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162202)

[source](https://x.com/jonatack/status/2111578122843828561)

Of the many things he mentions here, the one that stands out to me the most is that users might want a strong track record. 

I think a legitimate answer to Rearden's initial question of what it would take to get me to trust rbitcoin is time. When rbitcoin nodes have stayed in consensus for a halving or two, I might be willing to use it as a node.
